3. SKILLS AND TALENTS.name: 3. SKILLS AND TALENTS
3. SKILLS AND TALENTS.text:
ROLEPLAYING IS A CONVERSATION. The GM sets the scene, you describe what you do, she tells you how the NPCs react, you respond, and so on – back and forth.  The story grows one step at a time, and everyone lives happily ever after.

Yeah, just kidding about that last part.  Not on the Frontier, you don’t.

Sooner or later, the shit – just like prisoner Murphy – hits the fan.  Things come to a head, a point of no return is reached, and a problem mounts that cannot just be settled by talking your way out of it.

That’s when you call upon your mad skills.  Just break out the dice and show Mother you know a thing or two.

USING SKILLS

THERE ARE TWELVE SKILLS in total in the game.  Three skills are typically linked to each of the four attributes: Strength, Agility, Wits, and Empathy.  Skills are measured in skill levels, from 0 to 5.  You can increase your skill levels during play (DEVELOPING YOUR CHARACTER ).

Dice

Two types of six-sided dice are used in this game: base dice and stress dice.  You can use any normal six-sided dice if you don’t have access to the custom dice for the game, but it helps if you have them in two different colors to tell base dice and stress dice apart.

When To Roll

Generally, the rules in this book or the adventure text will indicate when to roll dice and what skill to roll for.  However, the GM can always call for a roll in a situation she feels warrants it.  We recommend against excessive dice rolling however, saving the rolls for dramatic and tense situations where something is truly at stake.

  Means Success

To use a skill, add your skill level to your score in the attribute linked to the skill, and grab that many base dice.  Then roll all the dice together. For your action to succeed, you must roll at least one 6 (  on the custom dice) – if not, your action fails.

Stress Dice: If you have stress level 1 or higher, add this number of stress dice to the dice pool as well. If you roll a 1 on one or more stress dice (   on the custom dice), you suffer a stress response – see Stress Response.

Rolls Without Skill: If you don’t have the skill required for the particular action you want to perform, you can roll anyway – simply roll a number of base dice equal to your attribute as well as any stress dice.

THE 12 SKILLS

  • Heavy Machinery (Strength)
  • Stamina (Strength)
  • Close Combat (Strength)
  • Mobility (Agility)
  • Ranged Combat (Agility)
  • Piloting (Agility)
  • Observation (Wits)
  • Comtech (Wits)
  • Survival (Wits)
  • Command (Empathy)
  • Manipulation (Empathy)
  • Medical Aid (Empathy)

Non-player characters use skills in the same way as player characters, with the one major difference being that NPCs never push rolls.  This means NPCs don’t have a stress level.

The GM rolls dice for NPCs, but should only roll for actions that affect a PC directly – for example, if the NPC is attacking a player character or is attempting to save them.  When an NPC performs an action that does not directly affect a PC, the GM can simply decide what happens, without rolling dice.

If the GM or adventure text calls for it, you may need to use a different attribute than the one normally linked to a skill.  For example, threatening an NPC may use Strength + MANIPULATION instead of Empathy + MANIPULATION .  You can even suggest rolling for a different attribute yourself if the situation calls for it.  The GM has final say.  Note that some talents specifically allow a different attribute to be used with a certain skill.

Modifiers

The rules or the GM can modify your chances, adding or removing base dice for you to roll.  This is referred to as +1 die, +2 dice, etc., and conversely –1 die, –2 dice, etc.  You can never go below one base die.  Modifiers never affect stress dice.

Gear: Equipment can modify your roll, but not always.  Sometimes a specific item is needed just to perform the action.  Weapons and other types of gear are found in chapter 5 .

Helping

Up to three other PCs and NPCs can help you with a dice roll.  Each person helping you gives you +1 die, but they need to be in a position to actually support your action in a concrete way.  The GM has final say.  In combat, helping someone uses up your full action for the round.

The air scrubbers on the USCSS Miranda are offline and our roughneck Nat tries to repair them.  With Strength 5 and skill level 3 in HEAVY MACHINERY, she gets eight base dice.  She uses a maintenance jack for the job and Jeffries helps her out, giving her +2 dice for a whopping total of ten base dice.

Multiple Successes

The more    you roll, the better the result.  In combat (COMBAT & INITIATIVE ), that usually means more damage, but it can mean any number of bonus effects – for example:

  • You show off.
  • You do it quickly.
  • You do it quietly.
  • You achieve some unexpected additional effect.

The adventure text or the GM has final say on what extra can be used for.

Failure

If you don’t roll any    , you mess up.  For some reason, you failed to achieve your goal.  Feel free to elaborate on why with the help of the GM.  She might even decide that a failed roll has further consequences that will move the story forward in a dramatic way.

Failure should never stop the story completely.  Even when you fail, there must be a way forward – perhaps at the cost of time, risk, or W-Y dollars, but still a way.  The GM has the final say on the consequences of failure in any particular situation.

You have one last chance if you really want to succeed – you can push the roll.

Pushing Your Roll

If you fail a roll, or need more    , you can choose to push the roll.  This immediately increases your stress level (Stress Level ) one step, meaning you add one stress die to your dice pool.  Then re-roll all dice not showing    .  All dice count after the re-roll, including the ones not re-rolled.

Stress Dice: If you rolled one or more   on stress dice in the initial roll, you cannot push the roll.

Just Once: You can only push your roll once, unless you have a talent that allows you to push a roll a second time.

Despite good odds, Nat fails to repair the air scrubbers.  She decides to push the roll, increasing her stress level to 1 and adding one stress die to her dice pool.  She then re-rolls the ten base dice along with the stress die, now getting two    . She succeeds, and as a bonus effect for the extra    , the GM decides that she finds a strange icky trail leading into the air shafts ...

Stress Response

If you roll   on one or more stress dice in a skill roll, a stress response is triggered.  Roll a D6, adding your stress level and subtracting your Resolve score (Resolve) before comparing the result to the table below.  Your stress responses are removed by relieving stress (Relieving Stress ).  If you get a stress response that you already have, you instead gain stress level +1.

Passive Rolls

Sometimes, the GM will ask you to roll for something you’re not even aware of – typically OBSERVATION rolls in stealth mode (Detection).  Such rolls cannot be pushed, nor trigger stress responses.  You still add your stress level to the roll.  The GM can even make some passive rolls in secret.

STRESS CARDS

In the Hope’s Last Day Starter Set, custom cards for all enduring stress responses are included.

Opposed Rolls

When facing an active resistance to your skill roll, you need to roll off against your opponent.  In an opposed roll, you need to roll more    than your opponent to succeed.  You can push the roll even if you’re the target of an opposed roll.  Opposed rolls are used sparingly, only when indicated by the rules or the adventure text, or when deemed appropriate by the GM.

PvP: In the case of two PCs rolling off against each other, the active PC decides whether to push the roll first, and if so, re-rolls, then the passive PC decides whether to push or not.

Open Rolls: In opposed rolls where there is no clear active party, a tie means there is no clear winner of the roll.  If this doesn’t work in the situation, break the tie randomly.

Captain Charlize on the USCSS Miranda is attempting to bypass Mother’s antagonistic actions by accessing her core in the mainframe.  The GM says this is an opposed roll against Mother’s COMTECH skill level of 7 (the ship’s MU/TH/UR 7000 mainframe has no base attributes).  Charlize has no COMTECH skill, so she’s just rolling four base dice for her Wits and four stress dice for the current stress level.  Her roll comes up with one    , but the GM rolls for Mother and gets two    .  
Charlize decides to push the roll, increasing her stress level to 5 and adding another stress die to her dice pool.  She then re-rolls all dice not showing    , getting two more    for a total of three! However, she also rolls one   on a stress die.  With a Resolve score of 4 and stress level 5, she rolls a D6 and adds 1.  In a stroke of bad luck, she rolls a 6 for a total of 7.  The captain messes up! On the brink of triumph, Mother takes control of the USCSS Miranda and her communications.  As a result, Charlize gains +1 stress level.

STORY POINTS

In a cinematic adventure, you can spend a story point (Story Points) to automatically get a    result on one base die in a skill roll.  This can be done before or after pushing the roll.  You gain story points by following your personal agenda (Personal Agenda ).  You can never have more than 3 story points.

THE SKILLS

Heavy Machinery (Strength)

Hard work is part of life for any roughneck on the Frontier, but at least you have powerful machines to help you.  Roll for this skill when you attempt to use, repair, jury-rig or break any kind of heavy machinery.

Stamina (Strength)

When your physical endurance or vigor is tested, roll for STAMINA .  For example, this skill is used to survive the cold vacuum of space or to resist a deadly contagion.

Close Combat (Strength)

The world of ALIEN is a brutal place.  Sometimes, you have no choice but to fight for your life, up close and personal.  Roll for this skill when you attack someone in close combat.  Read more about close combat in chapter 4 .

Mobility (Agility)

Roll for MOBILITY to perform any kind of acrobatic movement such as a risky climb or a dangerous jump.

Piloting (Agility)

Be it a dropship, a star freighter or a battle frigate, you’re the one to fly it.  Roll for PILOTING when you attempt any difficult and dangerous maneuver at the helm of any type of spacecraft (Combat Phases ).  The skill can also be used to drive ground vehicles.

Ranged Combat (Agility)

If you have a ranged weapon, you can take down your enemy from a distance without getting your hands bloody.  Use the RANGED COMBAT skill to fire all types of ranged weapons.  Read more about ranged combat in chapter 4 .

Comtech (Wits)

Programming androids, mainframes, and other types of advanced technology requires specialist knowledge.  Roll for COMTECH for any challenging attempt to program, repair, decrypt or otherwise manipulate any type of computer or communications technology.

Observation (Wits)

In the world of ALIEN, you need to be on your guard at all times, or you won’t live long.  Use your OBSERVATION skill to spot someone sneaking.  You can also use the skill when you spot an unknown threat of some kind, to learn more about it.  Read more about stealth mode in the next chapter.

Survival (Wits)

Terraforming can make the atmosphere on alien worlds (passably) breathable, but it will rarely make them Earthlike.  You might be able to breathe without a pressure suit on such worlds, though you can also expect to struggle against extreme heat and cold, sandstorms, acid rain, and other extreme weather. Roll for SURVIVALwhen you’re in a hazardous environment to avoid becoming fatigued – or worse (Fatigue ).

Command (Empathy)

If you are to survive the horrors of space, you’ll need a good leader – or you must become one yourself.  You can use your COMMAND skill to stop panic in other PCs and to give orders in combat (Stopping Panic ).

Manipulation (Empathy)

Alien life forms may gut you without remorse, but the most truly dangerous beings in the ALIEN universe are corporate agents and other schemers who use lies, threats, or subtle persuasion to get what they want.  To make another person see things your way, roll for MANIPULATION .  If the person is actively opposed to your point of view, this is an opposed MANIPULATION roll (Opposed Rolls ).  Your chances are affected by your negotiating position (see the adjacent sidebar).

NOT MIND CONTROL

When you use MANIPULATION on someone, you don’t take control of their mind.  What you are trying to convince your adversary to do must be somewhat reasonable, or the GM can disallow it.

Medical Aid (Empathy)

In the world of ALIEN, there is a significant risk that you or the other characters will be injured, sooner or later.  Roll for MEDICAL AID  to give first aid to a dying character (Broken ) or to make medical examinations.

Your chances of using MANIPULATION on someone successfully are affected by your negotiating position.  
Each of the following factors gives you +1 die:

  • You have more people on your side.
  • What you ask for doesn’t cost your opponent anything.
  • Your opponent has suffered damage.
  • You have helped your opponent previously.
  • You present your case very well (determined by the GM).

Each of the following factors gives you −1 die:

  • Your opponent has more people on their side.
  • You ask for something valuable or dangerous.
  • Your opponent has nothing to gain by helping you.
  • You are having trouble understanding each other.
  • You are talking via radio or shouting at a distance.

TALENTS

TO SURVIVE AND THRIVE in the cold dark of space you need to find your own niche, something you and no one else can do.  Such special abilities are called talents.

Talents can affect how you use skills or how you recover from damage or stress, or even let you do things that are quite simply impossible for others. Unlike skills, talents are not rated – you either have them or you don’t.

There are two distinct types of talents – career talents and general talents.  Career talents can only be learned by characters with a specific career. General talents can be learned by anyone.  You can learn new talents during play (DEVELOPING YOUR CHARACTER ).

Colonial Marine Talents

  • Banter: The stress level of you and everyone in Short range drops two steps (instead of one) for every stretch of time spent in a safe place Relieving Stress ).
  • Overkill: When you roll 9 or higher on a panic roll (Panic Roll ), you can ignore the result and instead go into overkill.  All other PCs in the same zone must make an immediate panic roll.  While in overkill, you must attack your enemies on every turn and you cannot take cover, dodge, or defend yourself against attacks.  The effect stops when you or all enemies in sight are broken.
  • Precise Shooter: When making a supply roll for ammo (Ammunition ), you get to roll two dice fewer than your ammo supply rating, to a minimum of one die.

Colonial Marshal Talents

  • Authority: You can use your COMMAND skill instead of MANIPULATION to get someone to bend to your will.  You also get +2 dice to the roll.
  • Investigator: You get +2 die to OBSERVATION rolls when actively searching for something hidden in a zone (Hiding ).  This does not apply to passive OBSERVATION rolls.
  • Subdue: When attempting to grapple an opponent in close combat (Grappling ), you get +2 dice.  >
“Unfortunately, quotas have been raised to 20,400 hours, so you’ll be released from contract in another five to six years.  Thank you, and remember the company is really grateful for your ongoing service.”
W-Y Officer  

Company Agent Talents

  • Company Resources: Once per act in cinematic play or once per session in campaign play, you may gain +1 stress level to produce an item of your choice – you had it all along! It can be any item from chapter 5 , or anything else the GM deems reasonable, but it cannot be larger than a regular item (weight 1).  The item is not yours – the Company will want it back.
  • Cunning: You can roll for MANIPULATION using Wits instead of Empathy.
  • Personal Safety: If you are attacked and another PC or friendly NPC is within Short range, make a MANIPULATIONroll (no action) to make the other character be targeted by the attack instead of you.  Stress level +1 for each use.

Kid Talents

  • Hard to Catch: You get +2 dice to MOBILITY when dodging an attack (Dodging ).
  • Lucky: You get to re-roll any death roll or roll for a critical injury once (Critical Injuries ).  Choose the result you prefer.
  • Nimble: You can push a skill roll using Agility twice.  Stress level +1 for each push.

Medic Talents

  • Field Medic: You get +2 dice when rolling for MEDICAL AID  to give first aid (Broken ).
  • Nurse: When you tend to a character recovering from a critical injury (Critical Injuries ), each day counts double.  For each shift spent per day, you can tend to a number of patients equal to your MEDICAL AID  skill level.
  • Surgeon: You get +2 dice when rolling for MEDICAL AID  to treat a critical injury that requires surgery.

Officer Talents

  • Field Commander: You can use COMMAND to give orders in combat (Giving Orders ) as a quick action instead of a full action.
  • Frontline Leader: You get +2 dice to COMMAND rolls to rally a broken character (Broken).
  • Pull Rank: You can use your COMMAND skill to order other non-officer NPCs around, as long as they belong to the same organization as you.  If successful, the target must follow your order, even if it means harm or danger to themselves. Stress level +1 for each use.

Pilot Talents

  • Full Throttle: When piloting a spacecraft, you get +2 die to PILOTING rolls for accelerating or decelerating (Combat Phases ).
  • Like The Back Of Your Hand: You get a +2 dice to all PILOTING rolls for one specific ship or vehicle model (see chapter 5 ).  You can choose this talent several times, once per vehicle model.
  • Reckless: You may take +1 stress level before making a skill roll, before pushing.  You can push the roll normally, gaining another +1 stress level.

Roughneck Talents

  • Resilient: Roll for Strength (attribute only) any time you suffer damage.  You can’t push the roll, which does not count as an action.  For every    you roll, one point of damage is eliminated.
  • Steady Hands: You can, if you want to, skip rolling one or two stress dice in any skill roll.  When rolling for stress or panic effects, use your full stress level.
  • True Grit: You can push a skill roll based on Strength twice.  Stress level +1 for each push.

Scientist Talents

  • Analysis: You can roll for OBSERVATION to gain insight into alien artifacts or creatures that you examine for at least one stretch.  For every    you roll, you may ask the GM one of the following questions: Is it human or alien? Is it dead or alive? How old is it? What is its purpose? How does it work? What problems could it cause? The GM must answer truthfully, but is allowed to give vague or incomplete answers.  A successful roll reduces the stress level of all other PCs within Short range 1 step, while a failed roll increases their stress levels by 1.  Only one attempt is allowed per examined object.
  • Inquisitive: You can push a skill roll based on Wits twice.  Stress level +1 for each push.
  • Xenomorphology: When facing an extraterrestrial creature of any kind, you may make an OBSERVATIONroll (quick action).  If successful, you realize a potential weakness of the creature, if it has any.  If you fail, gain stress level +1.  Only one attempt per Xenomorph is allowed.
“There’s no bloody way I’m three months pregnant.”
“Well, doctor, it’s not exactly a traditional fetus.”
Shaw and David  

General Talents

  • Bodyguard: If someone in the same zone as you is hit by an attack, you can spend a quick action to dive in to take the hit instead.
  • Bonus Shares: Gain +2 dice to MANIPULATION rolls when negotiating the payment for a job in campaign play (JOB GENERATOR ).
  • Calm Breather: When making a supply roll for air, you get to roll two dice fewer than your air supply rating (Consumables), to a minimum of one die.
  • Combat Veteran: In combat, you may keep your initiative card from the previous round instead of drawing a new one.
  • Counselor: Once per stretch, you can use the MANIPULATION skill to reduce the stress level of another PC in the same zone.  For each    rolled, their stress level is reduced by one extra step (in addition to the default one step, see Relieving Stress ).  You cannot use this talent on yourself, nor recover stress in the same stretch as you use it.
  • EVA Specialist: You get +2 to HEAVY MACHINERY  and MOBILITY rolls when spacewalking.
  • Fast Reflexes: When drawing initiative (Drawing The Initiative ), draw two cards instead of one.  Choose the one you want to use and shuffle the other back into the deck.  If several characters have this talent, carry out this process one at a time in any order you prefer.  PCs draw before NPCs.
  • Gunner: You get a +2 dice to RANGED COMBAT rolls when firing vehicle-mounted weapons or spaceship armaments.
  • Hardened: Your maximum Health score is increased by 1.  You can choose this talent up to three times.
  • Haymaker: You get +2 dice to a CLOSE COMBAT attack if you sacrifice your quick action for the round .
  • Martial Arts: When you attack or defend unarmed in CLOSE COMBAT , you can use Agility instead of Strength.  You can also make an unarmed attack as a quick action instead of a full action, but with −2 dice.
  • Last One Standing: You can rally yourself when broken (Broken ) by rolling for STAMINAyourself.  Only one attempt can be made.
  • Machinegunner: When firing a burst of fully automatic fire (Full Auto ), your stress level does not increase.
  • Menacing: When threatening someone to do what you want, roll Strength + MANIPULATION (instead of Empathy) and gain +2 dice.
  • Navigator: Roll for COMTECH when plotting a new course for space travel (SPACE TRAVEL).  For each rolled, the duration of the trip is reduced by 10% (round off to the nearest whole number of days).
  • Pack Mule: You can carry twice as many items as normal without being encumbered.
  • Quick Shot: If an enemy makes a ranged attack against you, you may as a quick action (reaction) try to shoot them first.  Take +1 stress level, then roll for both attacks simultaneously.  The shot with the most goes off first.  If both shots hit, the second shot is aborted if the shooter is broken.  If both shots roll the same amount of , both hit at the same time.
  • Rapid Fire: You can fire a pistol (chapter 5 ) as a quick action instead of a full action, but with −2 dice.
  • Second Wind: Anyone who tries to rally you (Broken ) gets +2 dice to their command roll.
  • Seen It All: Your Resolve score (Resolve) is increased by 1.  You can choose this talent up to three times.
  • Sensor Operator: Gain +2 dice when rolling for COMTECH to operate ship sensors (Combat Phases).
  • Spaceship Commander: In the role as a captain of a spaceship during space combat (Combat Phases ), you get +2 dice to COMMAND rolls for initiative and giving orders.
  • Spaceship Mechanic: Gain +2 dice when you use HEAVY MACHINERY or COMTECH to maintain or repair damage to a spacecraft (Ship Damage).
  • Stealthy: Others get –2 dice to OBSERVATION rolls when trying to spot you in stealth mode (NPC Movement ).  In groups, the talent has no effect unless everyone in the group has the talent.
  • Stoic: You can roll for STAMINA using Wits instead of Strength.
  • Survivor: You get +2 dice to all death rolls (Critical Injuries ).
  • Tech Savvy: When making a supply roll for electric power, you get to roll two dice fewer than your power supply rating (Consumables ), to a minimum of one die.
  • Weapon Specialist: You’re an expert at using a specific weapon model – choose one from the weapon lists in chapter 5 .  When you use this weapon, you get +2 dice.  You can choose this talent several times, once per weapon model.  You can be a specialist at fighting unarmed.
  • Zero-G Training: Your sense of balance is well adapted to an environment without gravity.  You don’t suffer any of the penalties to skill rolls in zero-G (Zero Gravity ).

4. STEALTH & COMBAT.name: 4. STEALTH & COMBAT
4. STEALTH & COMBAT.text:
FIGHT OR FLIGHT? That’s the big question, now, isn’t it?

You may feel invincible tucked away behind your cozy character sheet, but your PC is out there on the line – and they are damn well mortal.  Remember back in chapter 2 when we told you not to get your character killed? Consider this your second warning.

Often, it’s a better bet to run away and fight another day – assuming you’re fast enough to escape whatever thing is nipping at your heels.  Often, it’s best to just meld into the shadows and be all quiet-like.  Before releasing the safety on your pulse rifle, always ask yourself – is it worth it?

Sometimes you have no choice.  Sometimes that alien thing you thought was right behind you is already waiting for you in that dark corner you thought was safe.

Just coming face-to-face with an alien monstrosity can turn your mind to jelly.  You may only have a split second before the beast dismembers you and crushes your skull.

And alien species aren’t the only danger.

People on the Frontier are jerks.  Sometimes, someone just sticks a gun in your face.  When backed against a wall, you damn well better fight.  When someone or something comes for you, you need to be able to defend yourself.

Here’s how.

SPACE & TIME

“Should be in and out in thirty minutes.”
Tyler   

Maps

A stealth scene or a fight in the ALIEN roleplaying game is typically played out using a map of the starship, colony, or whatever location your characters happen to find themselves fighting for their lives in.  Large, full-color maps of adventure locations are included in the Hope’s Last Day Starter Set and cinematic adventures such as Rapture Protocol, but maps with less detail work as well, even quickly hand-drawn sketches by the GM are fine for more improvised play. Tokens & Miniatures: To track movement on the map during stealth or combat, you can use the cardboard tokens in official ALIEN RPG releases like the Hope’s Last Day Starter Set, miniatures such as those included in the ALIEN RPG Miniatures Set, digital tokens on your virtual tabletop, or anything else that works for your table.

Zones

The map is divided into zones.  A zone is typically a room, a corridor, or an area of ground.  How big a zone is varies – from a few steps across up to about 25 meters.  A zone is generally smaller in a cramped environment than in open terrain.  In official adventures, zone borders are indicated on the location maps.

Cluttered/ Open: A zone is either cluttered, meaning there are objects in the zone to hide or take cover in or behind, or open, meaning there are no such objects in the zone.  Open zones are typically corridors and crawlspaces, but can also be empty rooms or other open spaces.  If the adventure text does not indicate whether a zone is open or cluttered, the GM makes a judgment call.

PLAYING WITHOUT MAPS

Although maps can be useful, you can choose not to use them and let certain conflicts play out only in the “theater of the mind.” In this case, the GM needs to determine lines of sight and the distances between combatants.

Borders: A border between two adjacent zones is either open or blocked (by a wall or bulkhead).  A blocked border can have a door or a hatch, as indicated by the map, allowing movement between the two zones.  Corridors and crawlspaces are divided into several zones by doors or lines on the map.  

Line Of Sight: Except for characters who are hiding or in full cover, everyone in the same zone has line of sight to each other.  This does not apply to narrow crawlspaces like air shafts – there, other characters block line of sight (even friendlies).  Open zone borders don’t block line of sight.  A blocked border generally blocks line of sight even if there is a door or hatch in it – unless you’re actively standing by the doorway and peeking through.

Range

The distance between combatants is divided into five range categories.  See the diagram below.

Measuring Time

In the ALIEN universe, time matters.  Whether you are awaiting rescue on an alien world with Xenomorphs stalking you, or Mother is counting down to the imminent destruction of your ship, you need to keep track of time.

Three separate units of time are typically used in the game, depending on the situation at hand.  See the table below.  The exact duration of a round, stretch and shift can vary depending on the situation.

UNIT   DURATION   PRIMARY USE
Round   5–10 seconds   Combat
Stretch   5–10 minutes   Stealth
Shift   5–10 hours   Recovery

During a countdown to some catastrophic event, time can be treated as a consumable (Consumables).  The GM or the adventure text sets the timer to a certain number of minutes.  After each combat round, a supply roll is made.  For each   rolled, the number of minutes remaining is reduced by one.

STEALTH MODE

“If you don’t stay quiet, we all die.”
Andy   

IN THE ALIEN ROLEPLAYING GAME, much of the thrill happens before the enemy shows itself and bullets start flying.  A key part of the experience is exploring unknown locations, with enemies lurking in the darkness.  In the game, this is represented by what we call stealth mode.  Stealth mode is played out in stretches of time, each approximately 5–10 minutes long.

PC Movement

Movement in stealth mode is slow and careful.  In one stretch of time, your character can move into an adjacent zone on the map (assuming the border is open or has an open door or hatch), scan for enemies, and get a superficial description of the zone from the GM.  If you’re a team, you can move individually or as a group.  The order in which PCs move is chosen freely. Searching A Zone: If you want to examine something in a zone more closely, to search a room or access a data terminal, you may need to stay several stretches in the zone (or even a full shift), if the adventure text or the GM calls for it.

NPC Movement

In stealth mode, NPC movement is managed secretly by the GM each stretch, after your PCs have moved.  Human NPCs follow the same rules for movement as PCs, while Xenomorphs may move one zone per point of Speed (THE XENOMORPHS ) each stretch.  The order of NPC movement is chosen by the GM.

Active & Passive: An adventure text may tell the GM that enemies are active or passive.  Active enemies are moving across the map, stalking you or trying to hide from you.  Passive enemies are not aware of you and are most often stationary, until they spot you or are otherwise alerted to your presence.  Enemies may switch from passive to active, or vice versa, as dictated by the adventure or the GM.  

Hidden Map: To manage NPC movement, we recommend that the GM has a second copy of the map, hidden from view by the GM Screen.  On this map, the GM can place tokens to represent NPCs, hidden from the players’ view.  GM maps for this purpose are included in official adventures.  If the GM doesn’t have access to a screen, they can track hidden NPC movement on a piece of paper.

Managing NPC movement secretly by the GM in stealth mode is a great way to create real tension at the table, a true game of cat and mouse – or rather, a game of human and terrifying Xeno­morph! However, it does require some table space (or virtual tabletop support) and might not always be feasible. In such cases, the system can be simplified to only have the PCs move according to the stealth mode rules, while NPCs (and motion tracker pings) simply appear when and where the GM so chooses.

Crawlspaces

Air shafts and other crawlspaces are a common feature in ALIEN adventures and present a unique challenge in stealth mode.  Crawlspaces can run by the side of rooms and corridors, above them or underneath them (in which case just the outline is shown on official adventure maps).

Access Points: A crawlspace can be entered by one zone’s worth of movement at any access point marked on the map, just like entering any other zone.  

Sealing Access Points: An access point can typically be sealed shut with a cutting torch by making a HEAVY MACHINERY roll (full action, one attempt per stretch is allowed).  Not even Xenomorphs can break through a sealed access point, but acid blood will burn through a crawlspace floor in one stretch (if there is gravity), creating a new access point if the duct is above a room.

Open Zones: Zones in crawlspaces are generally considered open, meaning it’s not possible to hide there (or take cover in combat, see Cover ).

Detection

When you come within line of sight of an NPC in stealth mode, or vice versa, make a passive open opposed OBSERVATION roll.  This means the roll cannot be pushed, nor trigger stress responses (Stress Response ).  The GM will just ask you to roll OBSERVATION without telling you why, and roll for the NPC.  

If one side wins the roll, they spot the other first and can choose to declare their presence, ambush their opponent (Surprise & Ambush ), hide in the zone (below ), or back out of the zone the same way they entered.  Backing out of the zone in this situation is done immediately and does not count toward the normal movement in this stretch.

On a tied roll, you spot each other at the same time – draw initiative (Drawing The Initiative ).

Keeping Guard: If a person remains stationary in a zone for a stretch and does nothing except keeping guard, they gain +2 dice to OBSERVATION rolls to spot anything coming within line of sight.

Groups In Stealth Mode

When several characters moving as a group come into line of sight of another character (or group), all characters in each group get to roll OBSERVATION.  Only the best roll on each side counts.  For a group of NPCs with identical stats, the GM will typically make just a single OBSERVATION roll and apply the result to the whole group, to keep things simple.

Hiding

A character can hide in a cluttered zone (but not in an open zone).  To hide carefully takes one stretch, and thus cannot be combined with movement or searching the zone – except immediately after a (won) OBSERVATION roll when coming within line of sight of an enemy (see Detection, above).  In this specific case only, hiding is “free.” Items can also be hidden in a zone.  

Finding What’s Hidden: When an enemy enters a zone with a hidden character, no opposed OBSERVATION roll is made.  Instead, the enemy must actively search the zone for a stretch and make an OBSERVATION roll.  If the roll fails, another roll can be made each stretch.  Typically, an NPC will only search a zone for one stretch before moving on.  If a hidden character is found, draw initiative.

DARKNESS

In dark zones with very dim lightning, OBSERVATION rolls for humans (and androids) are made with –2 dice.  Xenomorphs are not affected.  A flashlight will remove the effects of darkness in a zone.

Multiple Searchers: If several characters search a zone at the same time, they can make separate rolls or let one character roll, and the others help (Helping ).  

Multiple Hidden Things: If there are several hidden characters and/or items in a zone, each    rolled on the OBSERVATION roll(s) will reveal one of them.  The order in which they are found is up to the GM.  

Taking Action: A hidden character may, at their turn in the stretch, take action to move out of the zone, interact with something in the zone, or ambush an enemy.  In all such cases, make an opposed OBSERVATION roll against all enemies in line of sight.

Motion Trackers

A motion tracker, such as the M314 MOTION TRACKER, can be used once per stretch.  This does not exclude other activities during the stretch, but before the tracker gives any information a power supply roll must be made (Consumables ).

If still powered up, the motion tracker will automatically detect the presence of all NPCs within its range (four zones for an M314), even if not within line of sight – but only NPCs who moved in the previous stretch.  NPCs who remained stationary in the previous stretch are not detected.

Tracker Pings: Mark the “pings” of movement from a motion tracker by placing tokens on the map.  Such tokens are included in the Hope’s Last Day Starter Set.  Detecting an NPC with a motion tracker does not mean that the PC has spotted it – it only means the players get an indication of where an NPC is present.

Nat and Hayes are checking out the abnormal engine readings on the USCSS Miranda while carefully looking for the unknown killer on board, moving zone by zone in stealth mode.  The GM moves the killer on her hidden GM map.  It is currently stationary in the engine control room.

After a few stretches, Nat and Hayes split up as the medic wants to look for a surgical kit.  On her turn, Nat moves very carefully into the engine control room, where a horrifying Xenomorph lurks.  A passive opposed OBSERVATION roll is made, and Nat wins! She takes a chance and decides to hide in the zone, under a control console.  

Now, as Nat is hidden and the Xenomorph is not actively looking for her, it does not get to roll OBSERVATION again until Nat moves out of hiding.  The GM decides that the Xenomorph moves on its next turn, quickly jumping into an air shaft.  Nat is free to come out of hiding to check the engine controls.

Starting A Fight

When a PC spots an NPC or vice versa, stealth mode ends, and initiative is drawn (below ).  Draw initiative even if the NPC is not obviously hostile – forcing PCs who act first to decide whether to attack or hold off.  Also note that PCs can exchange initiatives with NPCs or each other on their turn (see Holding Off below ).  Combat can also be initiated by an ambush (Below ).

Social Mode

When you stop to interact socially with NPCs, or just stop to relieve stress (Relieving Stress ) or chat among each other, stealth mode stops.  During social mode, the GM estimates how many stretches pass and moves NPCs on the hidden stealth map accordingly.  Social mode can also be used when you perform a task that takes more than a stretch to complete.  When you start moving around on the map again, stealth mode starts anew.

Hayes is in the Medbay when the Xenomorph enters the zone via an air duct access point.  The GM tells Hayes to roll OBSERVATION but not why, and rolls for the Xeno herself.  The opposed roll is a tie, and they spot each other at the same time! Stealth mode ends and combat starts.

COMBAT & INITIATIVE

WHEN THE ENEMY IS REVEALED, stealth mode is over, and combat starts.  Combat is played out in rounds, each approximately 5–10 seconds long.  At the start of each round, the first step is to decide who has the initiative – in what order the combatants will act during the round.

Drawing The Initiative

To determine the initiative, ten cards numbered 1 to 10 are used.  Such initiative cards are included in the Hope’s Last Day Starter Set, but you can also use ordinary playing cards.  Each player in the fight draws a random card at the beginning of each round, and the GM draws cards for NPCs.

The number on the card determines the order in which you act in the round.  Card #1 acts first, card #2 acts second, and so forth until everyone has acted.  Your place in the initiative order is called your turn.  Your “previous turn” or “your next turn” can occur in the current round or the previous/next round, depending on if you’ve had your turn in the current round yet.

Place your initiative card by your character sheet so everyone can see the order in which each person acts.  The GM puts their card (or cards) in front of them.  When all participants have had their turn, the round is over, and a new round begins by drawing the initiative again.

Xenomorphs have a Speed rating and get one turn – and initiative card – per point of Speed.  Read more under THE XENOMORPHS .

To make things simple, particularly in large fights, the GM can draw a single initiative card for a group of NPCs.  All NPCs in that group act on the same turn in the round.  The order among them is decided by the GM.  When a PC holds off to swap initiative cards, they swap initiative with the whole NPC group.

TOO MANY DRAWS?

Combat in the ALIEN RPG is fast and deadly, and rarely lasts longer than 3–5 rounds.  Drawing initiative every round gives a more dynamic flow of play, but should you find it cumbersome, you can draw initiative only in the first round of combat.  Holding off and swapping initiative cards can still be done.

Surprise & Ambush

If combat starts with an attack that the GM deems to be surprising, the attacker automatically gets the #1 initiative card in the first round of combat. The other combatants draw their initiative from the cards that remain.  With several attackers, they get the lowest (earliest) cards to distribute freely.  At the start of the second round, everyone draws the initiative as usual.

Ambush: A special type of surprise attack is an ambush, which is an attack on an unaware opponent.  Ambushes are usually the result of stealth mode (NPC Movement ).  An ambush also gives the lowest (earliest) initiative card to the attacker(s), and gives +2 dice to the initial attack(s), and the target(s) cannot defend against it or dodge it.

Holding Off

At your turn in the round, you can choose to hold off.  This means that you swap initiative cards – and therefore places in the turn order – with another PC or NPC (or NPC group) whose turn comes after yours.  They cannot refuse the trade and must take their turn immediately.  You cannot swap initiative cards with someone who has already had their turn.

Note: All rules effects that are triggered “on your turn” (such as death rolls, see Critical Injuries ) are moved in the turn order when initiative cards are swapped.  Your turn doesn’t happen until you use it.  

Interrupt Actions: Quick actions that occur out of turn (such as defending or dodging) are not affected by holding off – spent quick actions still count as spent, even if you get a new initiative number.  Even if you have spent two quick actions as interrupt actions earlier in the round, and thus don’t get any action on your turn, you can still hold off and swap cards when your turn comes – this can be useful to give another PC an earlier spot in the turn order.  

Xenomorphs (THE XENOMORPHS ) with a Speed of 2 or more have multiple turns in a single round, and therefore draw multiple initiative cards.  When swapping cards with a Xenomorph, you decide which card you want, as long as it comes after your current turn in the initiative order.  Xenomorphs themselves rarely hold off, but can if the adventure text or GM says so.

“LET’S ROCK!”
Pvt.  Vasquez   

ACTION & MOVEMENT

Full Actions & Quick Actions

Each round, you can perform one full action and one quick action, or two quick actions.

Full Action: This is typically an attack but can be anything you could reasonably do in less than 10 seconds that requires your full focus.  It typically requires a skill roll.  See the adjacent list for examples.  A full action can only be performed on your turn in the round.  

Quick Action: These are faster and don’t necessarily demand a skill roll (though some do).  Quick actions include movement.  See the adjacent list for examples.  Some quick actions can be performed out of turn, to interrupt the actions of opponents.  On your turn, you can save your quick action for an interrupt action to use later in the round.  If you perform two quick actions in the same round, you forfeit your full action.  

Action Reset: All actions are reset at the start of a new combat round.  Actions can never be saved from one round to the next.

Giving Orders

As a full action, you can bark orders to another character.  They must be able to hear you, even if via a comm radio.  Roll for COMMAND.  For every    you roll, they get +1 die to one roll later in the same round, but only for carrying out the order you gave.

MARK YOUR ACTIONS

To keep track of your actions in the round, a tip is to keep your initiative face-up and vertical at the start of the round.  Turn it horizontally when you perform a quick action.  Flip the card over when you perform a full action or your second quick action.  When the card is both rotated and flipped, you’re done for the round!

FULL ACTION   SKILL USED
Attack in close combat   CLOSE COMBAT
Make a ranged attack   RANGED COMBAT
Jump or climb   MOBILITY
Take full cover   -
Interact with a terminal   COMTECH
Use machinery   HEAVY MACHINERY
Give first aid   MEDICAL AID
Clearing a jammed weapon   HEAVY MACHINERY
Persuade someone   MANIPULATION
Give orders   COMMAND
Drive a vehicle   PILOTING

QUICK ACTIONS

  • Move into an adjacent zone
  • Move between Short and Adjacent range
  • Move to a door or hatch and peek through
  • Lock a door or hatch
  • Take partial cover
  • Defend against a close combat attack
  • Aim a ranged attack
  • Dodge a ranged attack
  • Reload a weapon
  • Pick up an item from the ground
  • Rally a broken character

Hayes faces the horrifying Xenomorph in the medbay, luckily drawing the #2 initiative card.  As the Xenomorph has Speed 2, the GM draws two cards for it, getting the #5 and the #7.  Nat over at engine controls is not aware of what is happening and thus does not draw a card.

Hayes could hold off to let the Xenomorph make the first move but decides to keep his #2 card and act immediately.  He spends his quick action running to a nearby comms terminal, and his full action to use it to scream for help, hoping Nat will hear him and get there in time.  Now it’s the Xenomorph’s turn ...

“Is this gonna be a standup fight, sir, or another bug hunt?”
Private William Hudson  

Foot Movement

To move during combat, you can spend a quick action to go from one zone to an adjacent zone, to move up to a door or hatch to peek through it (or take cover by it), or to move between Short and Adjacent range from a character (or item) inside your current zone.

Doors & Hatches: You can pass an unlocked door or hatch during movement without spending an action.  Locking a door or hatch is typically a quick action.  A locked door or hatch can be broken down.  This requires a close combat attack (full action) with +2 dice.  A typical metal door or hatch has armor level 2 and can take 10 points of damage before it gives in.  Electronically locked doors or hatches can be opened with a COMTECH roll (full action).  

Blocking Movement: You can, as long as you’re not broken (Broken ), block another character from moving past you.  As a rule of thumb, you can block a cylindrical volume 2 meters wide and equally tall.  To pass you, your opponent must either take you out or make a special close combat action (Defend ).  Blocking is not mandatory – you can allow friendly characters to pass you.  

Crawlspaces: In a narrow crawlspace such as an air shaft, you cannot move past other characters in the same zone – not even friendlies.  Xenomorphs often prefer to move through air shafts and other crawlspaces, but can move through rooms and corridors just like human characters, including opening unlocked doors.  

Dragging A Person: You can drag a broken or otherwise immobilized person with you when you move.  The person needs to be at Adjacent range, and you need to make a STAMINA roll.  If you fail, you remain in the zone.

Leaving Combat

You can attempt to leave a combat before it’s over by moving out of sight of your opponents.  If you do, and it’s not obvious where you went (GM’s call), your opponents must roll for OBSERVATION (no action) to understand where you went.  If it fails, combat is over, and stealth mode commences again (unless other PCs remain in combat).

If you are using official ALIEN RPG tokens or miniatures on a map that is to scale, mark Adjacent range by placing the tokens or miniature bases in contact.  If there is no way to move into a zone without placing the tokens or miniatures in contact, the range between them is immediately Adjacent (not Short), without a further move action needed.  
You can move into a narrow area on the map (such as a crawlspace) even if your token or miniature base is wider than the space you’re in.  However, if the tokens /miniatures of other characters make it impossible to place at least half of your token / base inside a zone (GM’s call), you cannot move into it.  Broken characters don’t count.  
You can block movement in an area covered by the token or the base of the miniature.  Several characters can be placed in base-to-base contact to block wider areas.

HIDDEN MOVEMENT IN COMBAT

In combat, movement is usually open for all to see.  However, in some situations, the GM may choose to keep NPC movement hidden in combat, using a hidden GM map just like in stealth mode.  All other normal movement rules for combat apply.

In the next round, Nat is aware of the Xenomorph and gets to draw initiative.  Sadly, she gets the #9 card.  The Xenomorph draws the #3 and #8, while Hayes – terrified and wounded but still alive – draws the #1 card.  Hayes decides to hold off and swaps his card with Nat, allowing her to go first.  She spends both her quick and her full action to move, running the two zones over to reach the medbay, just in time to face the Xenomorph.

CLOSE COMBAT

CLOSE COMBAT is any attack at Adjacent range, no matter what weapon is used (if any).  This is a full action.  Roll for CLOSE COMBAT to hit.  Close combat weapons can give a modifier to your roll (see chapter 5 ).  

Hit: If the attack succeeds, it inflicts the weapon’s base damage on the target, plus 1 damage point for every    rolled beyond the first.  Damage may be reduced by body armor (Full Auto ).  Unarmed attacks have a base damage of 1.  

Weak Spot: Against an armored target, you can aim for a weak spot, getting –2 dice.  On a hit, the armor level is reduced 1 step (after reduction for an armor piercing attack).

Defend

If you are attacked in close combat, you can choose to defend yourself against the attack, to avoid being hit.  Defending is a quick action, and you roll for CLOSE COMBAT.  You must state that you defend before the attacker rolls for their strike.  Defending turns the attack into an opposed roll (Opposed Rolls ) – for each    you roll when defending, you eliminate one    rolled by the attacker.  

Interruption: Defending is an interrupt action and occurs out of turn.  It does require a quick action however – if you have no actions left in the round, you cannot defend.  If you fear you will be attacked later in a round, it might be wise to save a quick action for a possible defense.

Special Attacks

In close combat, you may want to achieve something other than just harming your opponent.  You must state that you are attempting a special attack before rolling dice, and you cannot use any bonus dice from a weapon.  Special attacks can be defended against just like normal attacks.  If the attack succeeds, you inflict no damage but instead achieve the desired result:

  • Disarm: You wrestle an item from your opponent’s grasp.  You can keep the item or throw it into an adjacent zone as part of the attack.
  • Pass: You move past an enemy blocking your movement (Foot Movement ).  If successful, place your token or miniature on the other side of the enemy.
  • Shove: You push your opponent to Short range from you.  This attack can be used to shove your target through a door or hatch.
  • Grapple: You pin your enemy in a tight clinch.  See Grappling below.

Grappling

If you grapple your opponent as a special attack in close combat, they cannot move or perform any actions except trying to break free.  This is a full action and an opposed CLOSE COMBAT roll against you (Xenomorphs use MOBILITY instead).  While you are grappling, the only action you can perform (until you choose to release your opponent) is a grapple attack.  This works as a normal unarmed attack but cannot be defended against.

Restrained & Unaware Opponents

If your close combat opponent is restrained or unaware of you (see Surprise & Ambush ), they cannot defend themselves against the attack and you get +2 dice to the roll .

Firearms In Close Combat

Note that you can use a firearm even in close combat.  You still use the CLOSE COMBAT skill (not RANGED COMBAT) to hit.  As most firearms have a minimum range of Short (or more), you typically get –2 dice or more when using them in close combat.  Your target can defend against the attack normally.

The Xenomorph attacks Hayes again in close combat, rolling a whopping ten base dice and getting two    .  

Hayes tries to defend himself against the attack.  With Strength 3 and no skill level in CLOSE COMBAT, he only rolls three base dice, but with stress level 3 he also gets to add three stress dice.  He gets a single   and luckily, no   .  

Knowing a single hit from the Xenomorph will likely end him, Hayes decides to push the roll, increasing his stress level to 4 and adding another stress die to his pool.  The re-roll produces another   , meaning Hayes just barely manages to hold off the ferocious attack.

However, the re-roll also produces a    , triggering a stress response.  He rolls a D6 getting 6, adding his stress level of 4 and subtracting his Resolve of 5, meaning he’s really frantic, getting –2 on all skill rolls based on Strength.

RANGED COMBAT

WHEN YOU ATTACK SOMEONE at Short distance or more, roll for RANGED COMBAT.  You need to have line of sight to your target.  You also need a ranged weapon, even if just something to throw.  The weapons tables in chapter 5 describe a variety of firearms and other ranged weapons.  Most ranged weapons give a modifier to your roll.  Firing a weapon is a full action.  

Hit: If the attack succeeds, it inflicts the weapon’s base damage on the target, plus 1 damage point for every    rolled beyond the first (unless the extra    are spent to conserve ammo, see below).  Damage may be reduced by armor (Armor ).  

Aiming: If you take your time to aim carefully before squeezing the trigger, you get +2 dice to your roll.  Aiming is a quick action and can only be done at Short range or more.  The aim must happen on your turn, immediately before the attack.  This means you cannot do anything else in the same round.  

Range: Weapons have a minimum and maximum range.  Any attack closer than the minimum range gets –2 dice per range band below the minimum range.  This does not apply to attacks against unaware or restrained targets.  A weapon cannot be used beyond its maximum range – with the exception that you can fire a weapon with Short maximum range into an adjacent zone if you’re standing right next to a door or hatch to that zone.  

Weak Spot: Against an armored target, you can aim for a weak spot, getting –2 dice.  On a hit, the armor level is reduced 1 step (after reduction for an armor piercing attack).  

Target Size: Firing at a large target, such as a vehicle, gives +2 dice.  Firing at a small object, such as a terminal screen, a hand-held item, or a Chestburster, gives −2 dice.

Dodging

If you are attacked in ranged combat, you can try to dodge the attack.  This is a quick action, and you roll for MOBILITY.  You can only dodge if you are aware of the attacker, and you must declare a dodge before the attacker rolls.  Dodging turns the attack into an opposed roll (Opposed Rolls ) – for each    you roll when dodging, you eliminate one    rolled by the attacker.  

Interruption: Dodging is an interrupt action and occurs out of turn.  It does require a quick action however – if you have no actions left in the round, you cannot dodge.  If you fear you will be attacked later in a round, it might be wise to save a quick action for a possible dodge.

Cover

When bullets start flying, you’ll do well to seek cover.  It’s also very effective against explosions (Explosions ).  You can only take cover in a cluttered zone, never in an open zone – except by a door or hatch, which gives you cover against enemies in the adjacent zone.  There are two types of cover – partial and full.

Partial Cover: Taking partial cover is a quick action.  You expose enough of yourself to be able to see, and shoot at, your enemy.  When in partial cover, any ranged attack against you gets –2 dice.  You can dodge (above) when in partial cover.  

Full Cover: Completely hiding yourself from view is a full action.  Full cover breaks line of sight.  Ranged attacks are still possible but get –3 dice and the attacks must penetrate the barrier (Barriers ).  You cannot dodge when in full cover.  

Direction Of Cover: For the sake of simplicity, you don’t need to consider the direction of your cover, it’s assumed to protect you from all sides.  The GM may overrule this however, if the situation warrants it.

Friendly Fire

If you fire at a target Adjacent to another character and miss, you risk hitting the unintended target instead.  Roll for an attack with two base dice, inflicting base damage if one    is rolled and 1 additional damage on two    .  If there are several Adjacent targets, randomize which one is hit.

Ammunition

Ranged weapons require ammunition.  You don’t need to count individual bullets.  Instead, the ammo capacity of each weapon in chapter 5 works as a supply rating (Consumables ).  After each attack, make a supply roll for your weapon.  When the ammo supply runs out, you need to reload.

Conserving Ammo: If you roll more than one    for an attack, you can spend one    to conserve ammo instead of increasing the damage, meaning no supply roll needs to be made after the attack.  You cannot use this rule to fire a weapon with zero ammo left.  Reload: Reloading a firearm is a quick action, unless stated otherwise.  You need to track your available reloads on your character sheet.  

Single-Shot: Weapons designated as single-shot must be reloaded after each shot – no supply roll is made.  You cannot use extra    to conserve ammo for these.  

NPCs: For NPCs, the GM typically doesn’t make ammo supply rolls.  Instead, their ammo capacity is reduced by one step after each attack, unless they spend an extra    to conserve ammo.  The GM can overrule this at any time it is dramatically appropriate.

Full Auto

Some weapons in chapter 5 can fire bursts of bullets.  When you fire a burst and hit without pushing the roll, you can immediately make another attack roll, at the same target or another, as part of the same action.  If you hit again (without pushing), you may roll a third time.  As soon as you miss, or push a roll, the attack is over.  Each attack roll except the first gives you stress level +1.  You cannot make more than three attack rolls in a single action.

Ammo: When firing a burst, you must make an ammo supply roll after each attack roll.  You cannot use extra    rolled in the attack roll to conserve ammo.  

Aiming: If you aim carefully (RANGED COMBAT), the bonus will only apply to the first attack roll.

Nat, at Short range from the Xenomorph, raises her Rexim RXF-M5 EVA Pistol at the Xenomorph, using her quick action to aim carefully and her full action to fire.

With no skill level in RANGED COMBAT, she needs all the bonuses she can get.

She rolls six base dice (three for her Agility 3, +1 for her Rexim, and +2 for aiming) and two stress dice (her current stress level is 2), getting two   .  Nat could use the extra    to conserve ammo but decides to maximize the damage.  The Rexim has a base damage rating of 1, meaning the shot hits for 2 points of damage.

DAMAGE

IN COMBAT, you run the risk of being injured.  Everything from exhaustion to bleeding cuts and broken bones is summarized as damage.  How much damage you can take before being broken is determined by your Health score.  Your starting Health score is equal to the average of your Strength and Agility scores, rounded up.  The Hardened talent can increase your maximum Health.

Armor

To protect yourself from harm, you can wear body armor (chapter 5 ).  Xenomorphs often have natural body armor, and vehicles can also provide protection.  The effectiveness of armor is represented by its armor level.  You can only wear one suit of armor at a time.

When you take damage from an external attack, the damage caused is reduced by the armor level.

Armor Piercing: Against attacks designated as armor piercing, the armor level counts as 1 step lower than its normal value (to a minimum of zero).  

Weak Spots: Attacks in both close and ranged combat can be aimed at weak spots in the armor.  This gives the attack a –2 modifier, but on a hit, the armor level is reduced 1 step (in addition to any reduction for an armor piercing attack).

Barriers

Barriers such as spaceship bulkheads also have armor levels – see the adjacent table for examples.  When a ranged attack hits a barrier, the damage is reduced by the armor level.  If the damage is reduced to zero, the attack does not breach the barrier.

Breach Limit: For barriers (and vehicles, see Damage To Vehicles), if the armor level is higher than the base damage rating of the weapon (not just equal), after any modifiers for ammunition and weak spots, the attack cannot breach the armor, no matter how many    are rolled.  

Cover: Note that partial cover (Cover ) does not provide an armor level – only full cover will do that.  If you are in full cover behind a barrier and wear body armor, first apply the effect of the cover, then the armor.  

Collateral Damage: In some zones, such as next to an outer bulkhead of a spaceship or a nuclear reactor, a stray bullet can trigger catastrophic effects.  In such locations, the GM rolls one stress die each time a ranged attack that could potentially breach the relevant barrier (i.e.  base damage ≥ modified armor level) misses its target.  On a    , the barrier is breached.

Broken

If you drop to zero Health, you are broken – in effect, taken out of the action.  Immediately roll for a critical injury (Critical Injuries ).  If you’re not dead, you can make a single move action per round and mumble through the pain, but not perform any other actions.  You can’t go below zero Health, but any further damage gives you another critical injury.  While broken, you cannot gain more stress and never make panic rolls.  There are three ways to get back up after being broken, assuming you’re not dead:

  • First Aid: Someone at Adjacent range can administer first aid with a MEDICAL AID  roll (full action, modified for medical gear).  On a success, you are no longer broken and recover 1 point of Health per    rolled.  If you suffer from a lethal critical injury, you are also stabilized (below).
  • Rally: Another character in the same zone can try to rally you with a COMMAND roll (quick action).  On a success, you are no longer broken and recover 1 point of Health per    rolled.  Rallying has no effect on critical injuries.
  • On Your Own: If you’re broken (but not dead) and no one gives you first aid, you automatically get back up after one stretch of time and recover 1 point of Health.  This has no effect on critical injuries.

Recovery: As long as you are not fatigued (Fatigue ), you automatically recover 1 point of Health per stretch of time spent resting in a safe area (even if suffering from a critical injury).  First aid and rallying can only recover Health when you are broken.

CONDENSED CRITS

The Hadley’s Hope Starter Set includes a condensed list of critical injuries.  If you have access to this and prefer a more streamlined experience, you can use it even when playing the full game.

Critical Injuries

As long as you still have Health left, damage points represent fatigue, bruises or smaller cuts – painful, to be sure, but possible to overcome.  Critical injuries represent a much more dangerous form of injury.  These can maim or kill you.  When knocked down to zero Health, roll a D66 on the Critical Injuries table.  If you roll a critical injury you already have (result #14 and above), re-roll.

Death: If you suffer a critical injury listed as lethal, you must make a death roll after the listed time limit has passed.  If the time limit is round, roll on your every turn, right after you act.  A death roll is a roll for STAMINA (not an action), but you cannot push it, and you are not allowed to roll any stress dice.  If you fail a death roll, you die.  If you succeed, you linger on, but you must make another death roll when the time limit has passed again.

“Come on! That’s all you’ve got?
Is that all that you bite, motherfucker?”
Dillon  

BROKEN NPCS

NPCs can be broken in the same ways as PCs.  An NPC can rally or give first aid to a PC and vice versa.  However, dice are usually not rolled when an NPC aids another NPC – instead, the GM decides what happens.  The GM can also decide that a minor NPC who is broken simply dies.

HANDLING DEATH

The death of a PC can be traumatic but try not to see it as a failure.  Instead, consider it a dramatic peak in your story and then get back into the action as soon as possible.  In cinematic adventures, character deaths are quite common – and can be very memorable events in the story.

The Xenomorph, ignoring Nat, strikes Hayes again.  This time, he fails to defend himself and goes to zero Health, broken.  He rolls for a critical injury and gets 62 – a massive hemorrhage!

Nat tries to give Hayes first aid to stop the bleeding with a MEDICAL AID roll but fails.  Desperate, she then uses her quick action for a COMMAND roll to rally Hayes.  This succeeds, and Hayes joins the fight again.  

On his next turn, Hayes fights valiantly against the beast, shouting at Nat to get out to save herself.  Then make a death roll.  Sadly, the STAMINA roll fails, and Nat can only watch in horror as Hayes collapses on the floor, dead.

First Aid: To save your life when you have suffered a lethal critical injury, someone must give you first aid to stabilize you before you fail a death roll.  This is a full action and requires a MEDICAL AID  roll, modified for medical gear.  If you are no longer broken, you can try to administer first aid on yourself, but with −2 dice.

  • If the roll succeeds, you are stabilized and can stop making death rolls.  If you were broken, you also recover 1 point of Health per    rolled.  The other effects of your critical injury remain until healed.
  • If the roll fails, your condition worsens – the time limit is decreased one step, for example from shift to stretch, or stretch to round.  If the time limit was already round, you perish.

On Your Own: If you succeed at three death rolls on your own, you survive without help and can stop rolling.

Instant Kill: Note that there are three critical injuries (results #64–66) that kill you outright.  If you roll any of these, you’re dead.  No death rolls, no chance of surviving – you’re done for.  Some Xenomorph signature attacks (THE XENOMORPHS ) can also be instantly fatal.  Finally, if the damage from a single instance equals or exceeds double your maximum Health, you are killed outright.  

Healing: Each critical injury has a specific effect that you suffer during the healing time indicated, which is measured in days unless stated otherwise.  Several critical injuries can heal simultaneously.  Each day during which someone with the Nurse talent tends to you while healing counts double.  Note that you can recover all your lost Health points but still suffer the effects of a critical injury.  

Surgery: Some critical injuries require surgery before they start to heal – this takes a shift of time and requires a MEDICAL AID  roll (with bonuses for talents and medical gear).

Stun Damage

Some weapons inflict stun damage instead of normal damage.  Attacks from such weapons don’t reduce your Health – instead, when hit you need to make a STAMINA roll (no action) with a negative modifier equal to the damage inflicted.  If you fail, you can’t perform any action on your next turn, nor any quick actions until then.  

On your next turn, roll STAMINA again, this time unmodified.  If you fail again, you’re stunned until your next turn after that, and so on until you make a successful STAMINA roll.  The STAMINA rolls can be pushed normally, and armor works normally against stun damage.

PANIC ROLLS

BEING IN THE COLD DARKNESS of space will test your nerves even under normal circumstances.  Add horrifying Xenomorphs, and you really need to keep your nerves in check to avoid spiraling into a wild panic.

Stress Level

The mounting tension in your character is measured by your stress level.  It usually starts at zero and increases during the course of the game.  Your stress can increase in many ways, such as:

  • You push a skill roll (Pushing Your Roll ).
  • You or a nearby PC suffers a certain stress or panic response (below ).
  • A nearby NPC panics (as determined by the GM).
  • You fire a second or third burst of full auto fire (Full Auto ).
  • You become fatigued (Fatigue ).
  • A member of your own crew attacks you.
  • A person nearby is revealed to be an android.
  • Any unnerving encounter as determined by the adventure or the GM.
  1. Roll D6.
  2. Add your stress level.
  3. Subtract your Resolve.
  4. Check the panic response table.

Panic Roll

As long as you keep your stress in check, you can use it to your advantage.  But if the tension grows too strong it can explode, sending you into a wild panic.  You need to make a panic roll when any of the following happens:

  • You witness another PC become broken.
  • You see a horrifying Xenomorph for the first time.
  • A terrifying Xenomorph comes within Adjacent range (even if you have seen it before).
  • You witness another PC suffer from a certain panic response.
  • A truly horrifying event occurs, as determined by the adventure or the GM.

Resolution: Roll a D6, add your current stress level, subtract your Resolve rating, and compare the result to the table on the .  

More Panic: If you are suffering from a panic response and are forced to make another panic roll, you suffer both responses if possible.  In cases where two responses cannot be combined, the higher response takes precedence.  If you already have a panic response (or stress response of the same name) and roll the same again, use the next higher response on the table.

Stopping Panic

Some panic responses are immediate or last until your next turn.  If this is not the case, the effect remains until one of the following happens:

  • Another character within speaking range (including comms) makes a COMMAND roll.  This is a full action in combat.
  • You are broken.
  • One stretch passes.

Relieving Stress

For every stretch of time (5–10 minutes) spent resting in a safe area, your stress level is reduced by 1 point.  In addition, one stress response (Stress Response ) of your choice is removed for each stress level reduced.  You can’t make skill rolls when resting, and if your rest is interrupted, it doesn’t count.  A panic roll can also decrease stress, as can certain drugs (PHARMACEUTICALS).

Mental Trauma

If you have rolled a result of 9 or higher on a panic roll during a game session, make an Empathy roll after the session.  Roll for the attribute only, not using any skill.  The roll cannot be pushed.  If the roll fails, you develop a mental trauma of some kind.  Roll a D66 and consult the table below.  Mental trauma can only be healed during shore leave in campaign play (SHORE LEAVE).

64   Psychotic. At some point every Shift (GM’s choice), you experience hallucinations that give you +1 stress level.
65   Amnesiac. You cannot remember who you or the other player characters are.  
The effect must be roleplayed.
66   Personality Split. Create a new character with a different name, Wits and Empathy scores, a personal agenda, and a random talent.  You switch personality every time you gain stress.

OTHER HAZARDS

THE WORLD OF ALIEN is unforgiving, and there are many ways for your character to suffer and die.

Fatigue

If you don’t get enough air, water, food, or sleep, or if you are exposed to extreme cold or heat without adequate protection, you must make SURVIVAL rolls at regular intervals.  As soon as you fail such a roll, you become fatigued.  Mark this on your character sheet.  Being fatigued has several effects:

  • You can no longer recover Health.
  • You must continue to make SURVIVAL rolls at the same intervals.  For each failed roll, you suffer 1 point of damage and gain +1 stress level.
  • If broken by damage from fatigue, don’t roll for a critical injury.  Instead, make death rolls at the same interval as the SURVIVAL rolls.  First aid has no effect against these rolls – only removing the source of the fatigue will stop the death rolls.

Suffocation: If your supply of air runs out (Consumables), or if under water, you must make a SURVIVAL roll every round (in combat, the roll does not count as an action).  

Hunger & Thirst: As a rule of thumb, you need to eat and drink something every day.  After a full 24 hours without food and water, you must make SURVIVAL rolls once per shift.  

Sleep Deprivation: You must sleep at least one shift per day.  After a full 24 hours without sleep, you must make SURVIVAL rolls once per shift.  If you are broken by a SURVIVAL roll caused by sleep deprivation, don’t make death rolls – instead, you pass out and sleep for a full shift, impossible to wake.  Certain drugs (PHARMACEUTICALS) can help against sleep deprivation.  

Heat & Cold: How often you need to make SURVIVAL rolls due to extreme temperatures depends on the situation, and is decided by the adventure text or the GM.  It can be once per day, shift, stretch, or even round (in combat, the roll does not count as an action).  

Hypersleep: Spending any length of time in hypersleep will make you fatigued.  Hypersleep fatigue is remedied after one shift awake, assuming you eat a sturdy meal.  The effect can also be counteracted by the Hydr8tion drug (HYDR8TION).  

Recovery: As soon as the hazardous situation is remedied, you are no longer fatigued and stop making SURVIVAL rolls.  If broken, you can then be stabilized.  

Androids are completely immune to all forms of fatigue.

Vacuum

Space is a cold and unforgiving place.  If your ship suffers explosive decompression (below) or if you are thrown out of an airlock, your life is in extreme danger.  The absence of pressure creates gas bubbles in your blood, causing your whole body to swell up.  This results in crippling pain, all while the raw UV radiation from the nearest star sears your skin.

In a vacuum, you suffer +1 stress level each round and you must make a SURVIVAL roll before you can take action.  The roll itself is not an action.  The first roll is unmodified, but you get −1 dice on the second roll, –2 on the third roll, and so on.  A failed roll means you drop directly to zero Health and become broken.  Don’t roll for a critical injury – instead, make a death roll every round.  Nothing can stop these death rolls except escaping the vacuum.  

Climbing into a space suit quickly (full action) requires a successful MOBILITY roll.

Explosive Decompression

Firing guns inside a spacecraft is very dangerous.  If a shot misses its target in a zone next to an outer bulkhead that can potentially be breached by the shot (Damage To Vehicles), the GM rolls one stress die.  On a   , the barrier is breached.  If a character intentionally tries to shoot a hole in the hull, make a normal ranged attack with +2 dice.  

A hull breach is bad news for everyone.  The air will vent out into space at a rate of one stretch per affected zone, and the intense draft will require everyone to make a SURVIVAL roll on their turn to perform any action (this roll itself is not an action).  

Most ships will automatically seal off a breached zone.  Once the air is gone, anyone still in the vented zone will suffer the effects of vacuum.

Falling

Falling on a hard surface in gravity automatically inflicts an amount of damage to you equal to the height of the fall (in meters) divided by 2, rounding all fractions down.  In a controlled jump, roll MOBILITY – each    rolled reduces the damage done by 1.  Body armor does not protect you.

Zero Gravity

Most ships and stations have artificial gravity generators, but these can fail.  You can also find yourself spacewalking outside your ship.  In a zone without gravity, all rolls for CLOSE COMBAT, HEAVY MACHINERY, MOBILITY and RANGED COMBAT get –2 dice.  In addition, every move requires a successful MOBILITY roll (without the penalty), with failure meaning you spin in place and suffer +1 stress level.  The Zero-G Training talent removes all of the above effects.  

On the flip side, zero gravity allows you to move in any direction, floating through open air (or space).  And you never risk falling damage.

“I think we oughta discuss the bonus situation.”
Chief Engineer Dennis Parker
