Minor Systems

GL285B, Delorme colony was another rebellious UA system.  The USCMC solved the “Delorme Problem” by nuking the site from orbit.  They said they evacuated the colonists first, but few believe them.  

GL382 is a barren system where a religious order established a spiritual retreat called Temple – visitors are not encouraged.  

GJ11038 is another uninspiring system.  Fifty years ago, an independent colony, called Deadfall, was established on the moon of a gas giant.  No one has heard a peep from them since or has cared enough to check.

What’s Going Down?

Holding The Line

The UA wants to remain dominant in Tartarus sector, but are under-resourced to do so, exacerbated by the garbled message from 78 Nu Ceti, and the departure of the fleet to investigate.  They lean heavily on the ORDF and W-Y, but neither delivers the support they need.

Administrator Prescott Smith feels personally vulnerable, posted here as punishment for undisclosed misdemeanors – his career stands on a knife’s edge.  He will happily see recalcitrant colonies receive the “Delorme treatment” (and get nuked) rather than let them break away and fall under the control of another power.

The 3WE Making Their Play

The 3WE is determined to reassert its authority, by teaching Linna 349 a long overdue lesson, regaining control of Lebanon II and sowing dissent among the UA’s colonies.  The 3WE’s military strength is mustering around Fiori 16.  but developing asymmetric warfare options is top priority: the Xenomorph, Yellowbelly beetle, and Harvesters – all can do terrible, undeniable damage to the enemy.

The PCs get involved in these plots, as members of the 3WE, as mercenaries working for the right money, or bystanders forced to help through threats or blackmail.  They may be contracted to find specimens of the Xenomorph, the Yellowbelly beetle, or Harvesters.  They may work against the plots, or stumble across them as neutrals and must decide what action to take.

The UPP Wants In

The UPP wants to become a power in Tartarus sector.  They covertly support rebels on Linna 349, Lebanon II, and Torin Prime, but avoid open conflict in this sector of space.  Their number one priority is control of the dangerous but ultra-rich planet, Rodina.  The UPP has a scattering of Space Operating Forces and Cosmic Exploration Corps in the sector but are gathering more at 17 Phei Phei.

The PCs become involved in the UPP story by supporting or opposing them in their plans.  They may attempt to gain the UPP’s support for a rebellious group, or work to keep them out of the sector entirely.

The J’Har Rebellion

The J’Har President, Araceli Segarra, has a chip in the big game to exchange for help.  The J'Har need legitimate space truckers to get their rhenium to Argos, intermediaries to buy military equipment with the proceeds, and agents to work with the 3WE and UPP.

Para Guarani and his pirates operate from temporary bases, raiding easy targets, although Guarani has an audacious plan to capture a brand-new Conestoga cruiser.  Segarra and Guarani don’t see eye to eye, especially now that the UA has posted a bounty for his capture.  The PCs can help Guarani with his ambitious plans or take him in for the UA’s gratitude.

Someone the PCs know has been incarcerated in the GR161 camp, and they need to break them out.  Why were they incarcerated? Do they know something vital to the UA’s operations on Torin?

Trucking The Space Lanes

Life as a space trucker is tough.  Whether you’re paid-up crew knuckling under the Company for that extra share, or an independent outfit that’s in hock to the W-Y dollar, you’re always under someone’s thumb.  Despite the exploitation you still pull a few tricks: operating under the corporate radar you know how to keep things from your paymasters; you know the space trucker black market, for gear, information, and favors; you know how to play the system and get things done “off the books”.

Nothing moves without the space truckers.  Sometimes that means dodging local politics and petty blockades.  The PCs are contracted to move food, equipment, livestock, criminals, weapons, juvenile Harvesters, or some other dubious cargo.  Even if the Company says it’s okay, the ICC might take a dim view.  Maybe the pirates will fancy your sweet cargo too.

The Grass Is Always Greener

There are many systems to explore and planets to be colonized.  New colonists must deal with the superpowers or vie against a competing colony on the same soil.  Don’t forget to keep your bosses happy too.

For explorers and scouts there is plenty of work.  Quite apart from prospecting – their bread and butter – there are lost colonies to explore, suspicious activity to investigate ...  and rumors of lost space stations and ancient relics to follow up on.

The Glass Ceiling

Lunnar-Welsun has been held back by Weyland-Yutani long enough.  Now it’s time to break that glass ceiling and step out from Weyland-Yutani’s shadow.  Lunnar-Welsun’s Chief Executive in Tartarus, Melody Khim, is emboldened to keep pushing W-Y aside, employing the PCs to investigate W-Y’s activities.  Naturally, W-Y aren’t going to take this lying down, and their leader in Tartarus, Byron Stokes, retaliates in kind.

Where There’s Brass There’s Muscle

Don’t forget the muscle – the sector is brimming with conflicts for PCs with a taste for the rough stuff and the equipment to match.  Whether they are Colonial Marines or Royal Marines, the ORDF or the elite of the UPP’s Space Operating Forces, or colonists taking up arms against their oppressors, there is always a conflict brewing and the need for people to fight it.

JACKSON’S STAR

JACKSON’S STAR IS A REMOTE frontier colony on the planet LV-410 in the Alpheios system in the Far Reach of the American Arm Alpheios System ).  It has been supplying minerals to Earth since it was established in 2133.

History

The world was initially discovered by Jackson’s Resource Development Group, a freelance operation that has identified colonies on several other worlds throughout the Frontier.  Despite being rich in mineral ores, LV-410 proved to be a hostile and unforgiving world.  Its dense atmosphere cloaked the planet in thick layers of heavy moisture and clouds so dense that they block sunlight from reaching the world’s surface.  The atmosphere was also home to an ominous biological threat, a wind-borne microorganism that affected colonists in only minor ways to begin with, but over time mutated, causing ever-more serious illnesses.

Weyland-Yutani, which established the colonial operation on LV-410, attempted to mitigate the threat by building atmosphere processors across the colonized region.  Even so, in the colony’s early years, workers grew sick, with many dying of complications.  Recruiting fresh workers became difficult as stories of the planet’s lack of daylight and the threat of airborne sickness reached Earth, forcing the company to forcibly extend some of their workers’ contracts.

Life In The Colony

In the intervening years, the atmosphere processors have reduced the threat from airborne microorganisms considerably.  Both the population and productivity at the colony have increased substantially, but even so, the dense cloud layers still create a permanent darkness across the entire planet breeding isolation, depression and anxiety amongst the workers.

Nevertheless, with the colony thriving, some of the workers have extended their stay and even raise families there.  For those born on this strange colony world, they have known nothing else but darkness, rain, hailstorms and wind.

The Mines

There are four thriving mines located around Jackson’s Star, all extracting iron and associated rare metals.  These ores are crudely crushed and processed ready for transport into orbit by mining haulers such as the MODEL CM-93D MULE G-Class Commercial Ore Transport Vessel .  Once loaded onto a waiting Tesotek mineral refining platform, the mining hauler returns to the colony, whilst a commercial towing vessel pulls the automated refinery back to the Core worlds, a journey that takes up to a year.  During this time the ores will have been separated, refined and purified, ready for immediate use when they reach their destination.

Locations

Agricultural Area: Being so far from Earth, the colony's management maintains vegetable gardens in order to supplement the supply rations.  Workers in transparent plastic overcoats maintain the gardens lit by the orange arc lights that provide the much-needed sunlight for growth.  Part of the area is dedicated to several rows of enclosed hothouses.  

Atmosphere Processors: Jackson’s Star was built around the first three atmosphere processors on the planet.  Each one creates a localized environment in the lowest layer of the atmosphere by processing it through a fusion reactor.  They have (over several decades) scrubbed the air of microorganisms and reduced the incidences of sickness and death.  The huge cone-shaped towers form a menacing backdrop to the skyline and are lit up with glowing red anti-collision lights.  

Cargo Area: The cargo areas combine open concrete pads for the storage and stacking of shipping containers with dedicated freight warehouses.  Harsh arc lights illuminate the areas to deter thieves, and armed security patrols are frequent.  The great distance from Earth has made even humble consumables a valuable commodity at the colony.  An office complex at each location tracks cargo arriving from Earth and the few cargoes heading back to the Core Systems.  Spare shipping containers are often used to build walls, or as conversions into workshops or cheap colony housing.  

Landing Pads: Various landing fields have been designated around the colony for orbital cargo lifters as well as smaller personal flying vehicles.  The cargo lifters bring supplies and cargo containers down from the supply ships.  These fields are cluttered with cargo loading equipment and vehicles, maintenance carts and refueling bowsers, whilst ground crews work tirelessly to marshal the arriving and departing craft.  

Market Street: There are three Market Streets at Jackson’s Star.  Each is a hub of human activity, since the standard accommodation is so cramped, and workers like to get out and mix with their friends when off-shift.  There are a variety of neon-lit stores, bars and cafes, lounges, restaurants, strip clubs, and even outdoor play areas for children.  

Market streets are brightly lit places, with crowds of people jostling for space and sometimes getting in each other’s way.  Nevertheless, such areas are the focus of human activity at the colony.  Market Street areas also contain good quality housing units for supervisors, administrators and managers, as well as basic bunk-style accommodation for lower-level workers.

Mining Gear & Vehicles: Heavy equipment and vehicles are held in these areas for use at the mining sites.  This equipment is big, brutal and industrial and comes in the typical yellow warning paint scheme.  Most of it sits outside, exposed to the elements, but there are always maintenance personnel making repairs and modifications whilst underneath temporary transparent shelters.

Mining Sites: Mining sites C2 and G4 are the closest of the four mines in the region around Jackson’s Star.  Both are deep iron mines that are the reason for the colony’s existence.  Ore is briefly processed on site, ready for transport to the Spaceport Landing Area, to the east.  The mines work non-stop and spew steam and smoke into the atmosphere.  

Office Of Colony Affairs: Located along Central Market Street, Colonial Affairs is the Weyland-Yutani administration division.  It governs the colony, managing the mines, spaceport and atmosphere processors.  Colony Affairs has various departments including labor law, pay, workforce allocation, dieth, transport, infrastructure and franchise operations.  

Visiting the disinterested officials and clerks at Colonial Affairs, who sit behind armored glass under yellow-tinted strip-lights, can be a demoralizing and frustrating experience.  The bureaucracy shunts the tired colonists from one department to another.

Spaceport Landing Area: This large landing ground is used to transport ore up to a waiting Tesotek refinery in orbit.  Mining haulers take off and land every half an hour, on a continuous basis.  Occasionally, a huge starfreighter will land to off-load a large cargo consignment.  

Activity here is non-stop and frenetic.  Ore arrives from the mines via elevated conveyor tracks and is stored in huge cylindrical tanks, then chutes deposit the ore into waiting mining haulers.  The operation is coordinated from the Spaceport Control Tower, by the “Air Boss” and the “Ground Boss” (one responsible for landings, take-offs and ship turnaround, the other for ore storage and loading).  Even a small delay in operations will cost the colony millions of W-Y dollars.

Trailer Park Housing: Groups of colonists (or families) can move out of the bunk-style accommodations found around the Market Streets, to pool their finances and rent a “trailer hab,” a simple mobile home that can be moved to a new location by Colony Affairs as Jackson’s Star expands and grows.  There are three main areas of trailer park housing at the colony where these six-person metal habs are often crammed close together.  Each one includes cooking, sleeping and storage facilities and has electrical, plumbing and data hook-ups.  The widespread use of trailer habs indicates Weyland-Yutani’s lack of concern for the colonists’ comfort, and suggests they would rather ship in more of the prefabricated habs than build proper colonial infrastructure.

Adventure Hooks

Space Truckers: A valuable research specimen that survived the destruction of the Renaissance Station back in 2142 was missed by rescue ships.  Today, it is now drifting along with other pieces of scattered debris, unnoticed within the ring.  The PCs are a ship crew ordered to rescue a shuttle or ship crew that has gotten into difficulties near the ring.  The PCs might launch from Jackson’s Star, perhaps as a mining hauler crew, or as a supply ship crew heading back to the Core Systems.  Once on scene, the sample might be detected, or worse, the ship in difficulties has already picked it up, with disastrous consequences.  The great danger, of course, is to enter the ring, since it is made up of fast-moving grit, rocks and dust that are liable to rip holes in an unlucky starship.  The sample might be a Facehugger, it might be a complete Xenomorph drone, or perhaps a stasis box containing Z-01, a Xenomorph-derived pathogen…

“Right, take a good look outside the window ‘cause, the way I see it, we’re never coming back.”
Tyler  

Colonial Marines: The Marines are en route to the Solomons when their ship drops out of hyperspace into the Alpheios system.  Prepped and ready, their orders are to investigate an unresponsive Tesotek mineral refinery in orbit around the planet.  A mining hauler from LV-410 is docked but has not unloaded its ore, the hauler’s crew is not responding.  

The Tesotek’s telemetry showed unusual system malfunctions and a slight orbit change before comms went off-line.  What’s going on? Four colonists have stowed away on the hauler and entered the refinery via EVA in order to sabotage it.  These men and women have reached breaking point and want to punish Weyland-Yutani after their leader lost her entire family to a new virus outbreak.  The hijackers have killed or disabled the crew of the ship that got them to the refinery and are now sabotaging machinery that will result in it deorbiting and crashing into the colony below.

The colonists have also destroyed the communications array and reprogrammed the Seegson androids which will attack any Marine on command from the hijackers.  The Marines will face four colonists in Mk.50 Compression Suits armed with M240 Incinerator Units and Armat Model 37A2 12 Gauge Pump Action shotguns, as well as a variety of ingeniously repurposed mining demolitions equipment.  The hijackers’ greatest weapon, however, is the automated machinery of the refinery itself, from maintenance robots to environmental controls, elevators to mobile ore processing machinery.

Colonists: A Weyland-Yutani research outpost exists on LV-410 in order to study and monitor the various wind-borne pathogens within the planet’s atmosphere.  One scientist has discovered that an “antigenic shift” is taking place with several airborne viruses combining and merging their genetic make-up as a survival instinct.  

Whilst her colleagues are trying to harness this new phenomenon, she is certain that it is the prelude to a massive and catastrophic mutation which will see the airborne microorganism wipe out all human life on LV-410.  She has arranged to hand her data over to a third-party at Jackson’s Star but will be murdered during the exchange.  Who is the middleman? Who is the intended recipient of the revelation? Who is the murderer? Has the data gone missing during the murder? PCs might be witnesses assisting the Colonial Marshal, or might instead be caught up in the affair either for money or for reasons of public safety.

NOVGOROD STATION

NOVGOROD STATION (ICC registration: 1709556) is a 10,000-ton transfer station that orbits the star Alpha Fornacis.  140 personnel crew this lonely interstellar outpost which serves as a way station for long-distance freighters and survey ships as well as supporting in-system mining operations.  

The star system is dominated by a debris disc made up of millions of mineral-rich asteroids and planetoids.  Scattered mining outposts search for deposits of tungsten and trimonite.  Novgorod is typical of the small station designs currently available, perfectly suited to low-traffic regions and cheap to tow in and out again as the situation demands.

Novgorod is very similar to dozens of other Seegson stations established along the Frontier and it serves as a useful model for other small space stations.  As GM, you can use the layout and location descriptions for your own games, simply changing the name and/or location of the station to suit your current campaign.

Overview

Novgorod Station retains the “tapering spire” design of its much larger brethren.  It has a wide, circular engineering base (A Deck), upon which are stacked nine increasingly smaller circular decks, for a total of ten.  It can accommodate up to 40 visitors and can hard-dock with up to two starships at one time.  Additional visiting vessels must stand-off and await transfer via the station’s single Starcub-class shuttle.

Running through the center of all decks is the Transit Tube, which houses two passenger elevators, emergency stairs and a restroom, as well as conduits and service pipes running between decks.

Passengers are not allowed off the C Deck, the Concourse Deck, and the elevators will not operate for them.  The elevators will only open on G Deck if the correct security level is held by the crewman.  ID cards are slotted into the elevator controls to open the doors to that deck.

The A.P.O.L.L.O.  mainframe can be accessed from one of dozens of public terminals scattered around the station.  These terminals are wall-units, with a screen and manual keyboard, each requiring an ID card to be slotted in before coming online.  They provide access to the A.P.O.L.L.O.  mainframe, an in-station data and electronic messaging system, used as a library, data-log and administration and accounting system.  The terminals are also video phones, activated by lifting the telephone-style receiver and dialing with the keypad.  The image of the other caller appears on the screen.

OTHER STATION NAMES

  • Junction Station
  • Korosten Terminal
  • Carlisle Station
  • Platform KT3
  • Thetis Station

A Deck: Engineering

  • Engineering Platform: An open plan deck, giving access to the fusion reactor and its operating machinery.  There are two control stations close to the liquid hydrogen fuel tanks.  Two coolant tanks behind the reactor hold liquid potassium.
  • Fuel Tanks: Liquid hydrogen is stored here, used by the shuttle as well as forklifts, loaders and visiting shuttles.  They do not have the capacity to refuel an interstellar freighter.
  • Fusion Reactor: A 3.1 Gigawatt fusion power plant operating on a deuterium/tritium reaction that supplies power to the station.

B Deck: Cargo

  • Cargo Bays: Three cargo bays, serving as a supply store for the station.  Pallets and cargo containers are brought up from the starport via two freight elevators and maneuvered into place by a couple of power loaders and forklifts.
  • Airlock Access: An airlock for access to the exterior of the station, including an EVA prep area with pressure suits and equipment lockers.
  • Offices: Open plan admin offices, with terminals connecting to the A.P.O.L.L.O.  mainframe.
  • Colonial Marshal’s Office: The marshal and his deputy have an office here, as well as an interview room, well-stocked armory and four holding cells.
  • St.  Luke’s Medical Center: A small clinic, with four beds, an operating room, store, pharmacy and consulting room.
  • Workshop: Technical area with lathes, testing benches, racks of spares, and equipment.

C Deck: Main Concourse

  • Spaceport Lobby: An open area with check-in desks, an information point, and seating.
  • Spaceport Transfer Gate: Two arrival/departure gates and their lounges sit beyond the security desk, as does as an open-plan starport office.
  • Cargo Handling Modules: Cargo airlocks used for moving freight to and from docked starships.  The modules are connected to the cargo bays on B Deck via freight elevator.
  • Concourse: The heart of Novgorod Station is a wide-open, spacious plaza, with seating areas and video screens, lined with offices, cafes, a gym, restrooms and the Marianas Inn.  Opposite the Starport are the dozen or so stores of Galleria Nishi.
  • Promenade: Wide walkway with large windows looking into space.
  • Gym: Small gym used mainly by station personnel.
  • Security Station: Security monitoring desk and office, used by the two starport security officers to screen passengers.
  • Galleria Nishi: A dozen or so stores providing essentials and luxuries for station personnel as well as transiting passengers – clothing, personal electronics, tools, food, jewelry, bathing products, shoes, magazines and many other items.
  • Restaurant: This facility is called Maxine’s Diner and is open around the clock.
  • Marianas Inn: Small, twenty-room inn used by visitors or transiting passengers.  All rooms have en-suite facilities.  A laundry room, office, and reception desk are included.

Mallory Bourne

Chief Loadmaster

Mallory was dropped into the job and her crew of male loadmasters didn’t want her there.  But she’s mean and tough and threatened dismissals, marking a line in the sand.  Now she runs the cargo bay with an iron hand, and she looks after the other loadmasters when management starts giving them a hard time.  Mallory keeps her eye on every piece of cargo and every ship movement, spotting anomalies, unusual Seegson shipments and unregistered flights.

What is going on?

ATTRIBUTES: Strength 5, Agility 4, Wits 3, Empathy 2
HEALTH: 5
SKILLS: CLOSE COMBAT 1, HEAVY MACHINERY 4, STAMINA 3, COMMAND 2
TALENT: Resilient
GEAR: Maintenance jack

Jonathon Otaka

Marshal

Otaka is in his late 40s, and Novgorod is his seventh station posting.  He’s good at this job, and in particular, at training-up his deputies to cope with the unique crimes and challenges on the Outer Rim.  He is the kind of person who remembers everyone’s name and knows everyone’s business. If ever caught with his back against the wall, plenty of station staff would volunteer to help him out.

ATTRIBUTES: Strength 4, Agility 3, Wits 4, Empathy 3
HEALTH: 4
SKILLS: CLOSE COMBAT 2, RANGED COMBAT 2, OBSERVATION 4, MANIPULATION 2
TALENT: Subdue
GEAR: .357 Magnum revolver, flashlight, Armat Model 37A2 12 gauge pump action shotgun

D Deck: Life Support

  • Garden: A hydroponic garden, separated from the rest of the deck by large, clear windows.  It is used not for enjoyment or agriculture, but as a supplementary oxygen and water treatment system.
  • Water Tanks: Drinking water is stored here.
  • Life Support Bay: Sewage is treated and recycled into water, used water is recycled, and air is scrubbed and recirculated from here.

E Deck: Habitation

  • Crew Cabins: Basic crew cabins, each with bed, toilet, shower, station-to-station videophone, desk, and storage units.  A standard terminal gives access to the A.P.O.L.L.O.  network, including various pre-recorded entertainment channels.  A kitchenette allows simple meals to be prepared.  This deck is double height, with stairs leading to a second level of crew cabins.
  • Mini Market: Small convenience store for the use of station personnel who often buy food that can be cooked back in their cabin.
  • Restaurant: A staff-only bar and grill called Drifters.

F Deck: Lower Tower

  • Shuttle Hangar: Houses a Starcub shuttle, with space adjacent for maintenance and cargo loading.
  • Fuel Processor: Pumps for transferring liquid hydrogen fuel from a tanker, and processors for refining it.

G Deck: Upper Tower

  • Operations Center: Open-plan nerve center and command post for the station, set out like the cluttered bridge of a starship.  Around six personnel are here each shift, running the station from day-to-day.  Spiral stairs lead down to admin, allowing staff to move easily between the two.
  • A.P.O.L.L.O.  Mainframe: The A.P.O.L.L.O.  mainframe servers are located here, adjacent to the operations center.  The room includes a direct access and programming terminal.
  • Restaurant: An exclusive eatery called Bistro Hibachi.

H–I Deck: Science Labs

  • Laboratories: Multi-function labs, generously furnished with equipment, rented by Gustafsson Enterprise (H Deck) and the Seegson Corporation (I Deck).
  • Emergency Operations Center: A back-up ops center, usually locked and disused.

J Deck: Comms

  • Avionics: Sensor equipment and communications electronics bays.
  • Probe Bay: Robotic science probes are launched from this bay.

Dr.  Alicia Svenson

Seegson Scientist

Dr Svenson is a talented electronics and cybernetic engineer who helped to upgrade the Novgorod mainframe from its antiquated TYPHON server to the cutting-edge A.P.O.L.L.O.  system.  Svenson’s work at Novgorod is devoted to top secret bioelectric and AI software and A.P.O.L.L.O.  is a testbed for a whole new line of Seegson intelligent computers.  She is passionate and very protective of her work, believing that Professor Arnuld Keenes, the Seegson Chief Scientist, is untrustworthy and incompetent.  She wants his job and wants the kudos of perfecting the A.P.O.L.L.O.  product for herself.

ATTRIBUTES: Strength 2, Agility 4, Wits 5, Empathy 3
HEALTH: 3
SKILLS: MOBILITY 2, OBSERVATION 4, COMTECH 4, MANIPULATION 3
TALENT: Xenomorphology
GEAR: Seegson System Diagnostic Device

Sergei Morozov

Engineering Chief

A dour but hard-working engineering chief, he runs his crew ragged chasing down malfunctions, carrying out daily maintenance and swapping out machine parts for routine testing.  He commands an efficient department of 20 technicians and engineers but is always upsetting management.  Morozov pushes his nose where it’s not wanted, believing a lot of what goes on in Novgorod to be his business – and it isn’t.  This creates a clash with all the other department heads.

ATTRIBUTES: Strength 4, Agility 3, Wits 4, Empathy 3
HEALTH: 5
SKILLS: CLOSE COMBAT 1, HEAVY MACHINERY 4, STAMINA 1, COMTECH 2, COMMAND 2
TALENT: Hardened
GEAR: Maintenance jack, Seegson P-DAT

Events

Unexpected events may provide interest or might signal the start of some crisis.

The Ship: A mysterious ship has pulled up outside the station and the shuttle has transferred the crew on board.  But no one knows where they are or what is going on.  In fact, the Weyland-Yutani ship has no crew – none living, anyway.  A twitchy android (an early Hyperdyne model 120-A2) has killed the entire crew, all down to conflicting orders that forbade it from revealing the true nature of the company mission.  The android, Glynn, has been removed for study by the Seegson science lab, and the bodies are shortly due for disposal in space from the shuttle.  The nature of the ship’s mission is, however, still classified or unknown.

Secrets: The player characters stumble upon an on-station secret, perhaps involving the top-secret mainframe experiments involving A.P.O.L.L.O.  (See Dr.  Alicia Svenson below).  The PCs can try to profit from this secret, which may involve a risk of fines, imprisonment or even death.  

Jailbreak: The PCs are approached by a pilot.  His buddy (a ship’s engineer) has been arrested for fighting in the bar and is likely to miss his ship’s departure – losing him his job.  Can they provide some kind of diversion to confuse or mislead the marshals, while the pilot frees the engineer from his cell down on B Deck? They will be amply compensated to the tune of thousands of dollars.  The pilot is lying, the engineer has just turned state’s evidence against his shipping company, and the pilot has orders to assassinate him in his cell.  If the PCs assist, the pilot will vanish, leaving them to carry the can.  

Shadow Games: A PC has a personal item stolen from his room, perhaps a gun or camera, a flashlight, or bag.  Then something is stolen from their ship, or from the room of another PC.  Are they being targeted? Why are these items being stolen? They must work with Marshal Otaka to catch the culprits, made harder by the investigation of a deluge of anti-Seegson graffiti across the station.  There is a covert agent on-board, hired by Weyland-Yutani, who believes the PCs have been stealing company data and selling it on, possibly here at Novgorod.  The agent is blackmailing one of the shuttle pilots who helped him get access to their ship, currently standing off from the station.  He believes the data is hidden amongst personal items.  When a Seegson agent contacts the group wanting to purchase their “data” things should get more confusing – and dangerous.  Seegson believes, rightly or wrongly, that the PCs are data thieves and wants what they have!

Strike: The spaceport shuts down because of a loaders’ strike due to a management dispute.  This causes alarm, arguments in the concourse and urgent talks behind closed doors.  The chief loadmaster, Mallory Bourne, is fighting the loaders’ cause.  There are some who are desperate to get off the station, perhaps because they have committed a crime.  Will the PCs be tempted to help them? What other situations might occur during this worrying time? How is the Marshal managing the disruption?

12. LIFE PATH.name: 12. LIFE PATH
12. LIFE PATH.text:
LIFE PATHS

THIS LIFE PATH GENERATOR randomly determines most aspects of your PC’s early life, with a few choices for you to make along the way.  The circumstances and events revealed by the dice form the framework of your PC’s backstory, leaving you to interpret those events and fill in the gaps in any way you want.  

The life path system produces a wide variety of character outcomes and histories and can result in unbalanced PCs.  However, there is huge enjoyment in playing a PC whose backstory has dealt them a challenging hand, especially when your PC overcomes their disadvantages to prove the doubters wrong.

The life path does not use the concept of a key attribute, but your choice of career still defines the skills and talents available to you.

Human Or Android?

Roll 2D6.  On a result of 11 or 12, you are an android.  If you are an android, decide with your GM if you are a secret android (Attributes ).

Base Attribute Scores

Humans start with a base score of 2 in each attribute.  Androids may add +3 to two attributes of their choice before starting their life path.  Don’t worry about the low scores – you gain more attribute points as you progress through life.

Maximum And Minimum Scores

By the end of the life path, a human PC must have a score of at least 2 in every attribute and cannot have any score greater than 5.

Android PCs can finish their life paths with attribute scores up to 8.

Skill levels can never exceed 5 for any PC.  If the random life path roll results in an attribute score or skill level outside of the allowed range, re-roll or choose another result.

Follow these steps to determine the life path of your character:

  1. Determine if you are human or an android.
  2. Roll for your origin and gain 3 points in random general skills.
  3. Determine your early life, gaining 2 attribute points and 2 skill points.
  4. Experience a life event – roll to see what befalls you and gain 2 more attribute points and 2 points in random general skills.
  5. Gain 2 points in attributes of your choice and then apply for your first career.  If successful, you gain 2 points in random career skills, a roll for gear, and a roll for your first paycheck.
  6. Serve your first term – roll to see where you were posted and how well you performed.  You gain 1 more point in a random career skill, a random talent, another roll for gear, and another paycheck roll.
  7. Did you want to serve a second and third term? Follow the same process for your first term, but for each extra term you must reduce an attribute of your choice by 1 point.
  8. Get your psych evaluation.
  9. The final touches – your PC’s name, appearance, age, personal agenda, signature item, buddy and rival.

Origin

Which super-nation were you born into or which one made you? What is your corporate or government sub-affiliation? Where do you call home? Roll 2D6 on the table below to find out, then D6 twice for your sub-affiliation and home.  Finally, gain 3 points in random general skills (Random General Skills).

Early Life

What was your early life like, who did you share it with, and what experiences did you have? Roll D66 three times on the table on @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.SCl1BZa4oHjMeZ4Q]{EV - 32.  LIFE PATH - EARLY LIFE}

, once for each column, and add the specified attribute and skill points (2 of each) to your scores.  Decide the precise details of your early life experience, depending on whether you are human or an android.  You may also gain modifiers to your psych evaluation roll – note these as you go.

Life Event

Your life event can take place at any point in the lifepath of your choosing, but is decided now by a D66 roll on the table below.  These events offer story hooks and may leave a lasting impact on your PC – the impact should be roleplayed.  Agree to the specific details of any event with your GM.  Your life event gives you 2 specified attribute points and 2 points in random general skills (Random General Skills).

Career

Next, gain 2 points in attributes of your choice and then apply for your first career.  The table below lists the minimum attribute scores for each career.  To apply, make a skill roll against one of the skills listed for the career.  The roll cannot be pushed.

  • If unsuccessful, you are rejected and must apply to a different career (however, you may pull a fast one, see above).
  • If you roll one    you join as a standard recruit.
  • If you roll two or more    someone has noted your potential, and you gain a favor – make a roll on the table below.

PULL A FAST ONE

If you fail an application, you can pull a fast one.  Your PC does something underhanded or illegal to get around the system, or begs a favor from someone in the hierarchy – settle the details with the GM.  Your previously unsuccessful roll now counts as one success, and you’re in! But a dangerous secret now hangs over you, or you owe someone a big favor.

PLAYING A KID

The Kid is not a career, it’s a lifestyle.  You don’t need to apply to play a Kid, you may just choose this career.  However, Kids are limited to only one term for their career, while the other careers can be extended up to three terms.

2D6   FAVOR
1   Popular. Gain +1 bonus to MANIPULATION when dealing with your organization.
2   Free Rein In The Company Warehouse. Make an additional gear roll for your career.
3   Generalist Training Program. You gain 1 point in a random general skill, but owe someone a favor for getting you in.
4   Specialist Training Program. You gain 1 point in a random career skill, but owe someone a favor for getting you in.
5   Bonus. Make an additional paycheck roll.  But don’t let this success go to your head, as others envy you.
6   New Friend. Someone owes you a favor.  But are they really your pal? Can you trust them?

You’re Hired!

Once recruited, you go into basic training, get geared up, and get your first paycheck.

  • Roll D3 twice on the table below for career skills, gaining 1 skill level for each roll.
  • Roll once on the gear table for your career (see chapter 2 ).  Re-roll if you roll an item you already have.
  • Roll for your first paycheck.

Career Terms

You must serve at least one term in your career but may choose to serve up to three (with the exception of the Kid career, which can only serve one).  Follow these steps for each term:

  1. Posting: What did you do during this term? Roll D6 on the relevant table for your career on Career Postings to find out.  This can give you a bonus gear roll, and you also gain 1 point in a random career skill.
  2. Performance: How well did you do your job? Make a skill test against a career skill of your choice (you cannot push):
    • If you fail, you suffer a disaster (roll on the table above) and get –1 on your psych evaluation roll (@TEXTDRAW[RollTable.eJgLp3u3A5HAAHuY]{EV - 46.  LIFE PATH - PSYCH EVALUATION}

      ).
    • If you roll one    your performance has been satisfactory.
    • If you roll two or more    you have performed well and gain a favor (roll on the table above) and get +1 on your psych evaluation roll (Psych Evaluation ).  Re-reroll any favors you already have.
  3. Talent: Gain one random career talent (see chapter 2 ).  For your second and third term, you may replace this with a general talent of your choice.
  4. Gear & Paycheck: Make one roll for career gear (see chapter 2 ).  Re-roll any items you already have and make a paycheck roll.

Another Term? Should you choose to serve another term, follow the process for the first term.  However, subtract 1 point from an attribute of your choice for each extra term you serve – getting older and weather-beaten does that to you.

1D6   DISASTERS
1   Injured. By accident or someone’s design you are severely hurt.  Lose 1 attribute point from either Strength or Agility.
2   Trauma. You can’t forget a terrifying incident.  Lose 1 attribute point from either Wits or Empathy.
3   Lost Something. Lose a random item of equipment.
4   Misfortune. Someone dies, and you are blamed.  Branded a Jonah, no one will work with someone cursed with ill-fortune.
5   Nemesis. A rival stitches you up, and you are sacked.  Time to join the big bad world.
6   Sacked. Either through negligence or incompetence your contract is canceled.  Time to join the big bad world.

Psych Evaluation

Each character ends their life path with their psych evaluation, so the company can see what they’ve got on their hands.  Androids undergo a “product cognitive stability test,” and also roll on the table.  Players should roleplay the results.  Roll 2D6 on the Career Postings table below and apply any modifiers you gained during your life path.

Final Touches

Decide your character’s name, appearance, age, personal agenda, signature item, and buddies & rivals.  To complete this, keep in mind that your PC’s formative and life events may drive their personal agenda.  Good luck out there – you’re gonna need it.

2d6   PSYCH EVALUATION
≤0   Dangerous, unstable, volatile, prone to psychotic outbursts.
1   Flashbacks and hallucinations, unhinged and unpredictable.
2   Defensive, reactive to minor slights, prone to angry outbursts.  An untrustworthy worker.
3–4   Night sweats, nightmares, distressing outbursts.  Temperamental and self-pitying.
5–6   Mild trauma, nightmares, nervous episodes.  Disruptive, likely to bellyache and bitch.
7–8   Well balanced.  A good worker.
9–10   Positive and compliant.  Follows orders for an easy life.
11–12   Invested in their work.  Keen, ambitious, worthy of promotion.
13   Zealously enthusiastic, confident bordering on arrogance.  Too keen to please – what are they hiding?
≥14   Supportive of officialdom to the point of fanaticism.  Suspect use of illegal mood enhancers.
Warrants close monitoring.

13. LAST SURVIVOR.name: 13. LAST SURVIVOR
13. LAST SURVIVOR.text:
LAST SURVIVOR IS a solo mode for ALIEN The Roleplaying Game – no Game Mother required.  When you take risks, utilize your skills, and encounter danger, make rolls as normal.  When the outcome is unclear, lean on the tools presented in these rules to fill in the narrative gaps.

A Brief & Brutal Story

Last Survivor is intended for one-off scenarios.  Your PC may survive – but they will most likely perish.  Either way, focus on playing through a captivating story with high stakes and insurmountable odds.  Depending on the length of your sessions, you might wrap up a mission in a single session, or over the course of a few sessions.

CREATING YOUR ­SURVIVOR

When creating your character for Last Survivor, follow the guidelines presented in chapter 2.

Solo Survivor Talents

When selecting your talents, consider options that fit your character concept while also providing utility and survivability.  See the lists below for recommendations of talents to consider and avoid, but ultimately, choose the talents that best suit your character.

  • Ideal Talents For A Solo PC: Company Resources (Company Agent), Hard to Catch (Kid), Lucky (Kid), Reckless (Pilot), Resilient (Roughneck), True Grit (Roughneck), Fast Reflexes, Hardened, Last One Standing, Seen it All, Stealthy, Survivor
  • Talents To Avoid As A Solo PC: Banter (Colonial Marine), Personal Safety (Company Agent), Field Commander (Officer), Frontline Leader (Officer), Bodyguard, Second Wind, Spaceship Commander

Playing A Solo Android

Androids in the ALIEN universe often find themselves alone.  Because of this – as well as their increased survivability and resistance to panic – an android makes an ideal solo character.  To create an android character, follow the guidelines under CORE CONCEPTS.

Extra Talent

Your odds of survival as a solo character are low.  To create a solo character with better survivability, choose an extra general talent (General Talents).

Solo XP Rewards

Instead of the usual end-of-session experience rewards, solo characters earn XP as they complete objectives using an objective timer (OBJECTIVE TIMER).  The greater the starting rank of the objective, the more XP are earned when that objective is reached.  See for details on objective timers.  

MISSION STARTERS

Without a Game Mother, you cannot wait for the story to happen to your character.  Instead, kick things off with an immediate problem or goal.  Before you begin, determine what dangerous situation the character has found themself thrust into.  Use these versatile mission starters to jump right into the action.  Each mission is thematically tied to a career on the Frontier (CAREERS ON THE FRONTIER), but anybody can conceivably find themselves entangled in these scenarios.

Space Trucker Missions

  • Nobody’s Home: You finally touch down on a remote settlement after a long, dreamless hypersleep.  Your ship carries much-needed supplies for the colony, but you find the settlement deserted, seemingly abandoned.
  • Unearthed Artifact: The colonists discovered something ancient and alien deep below the settlement.  With the colony deserted, you must uncover the truth of the artifact.  >
  • Company Meddling: You quickly uncover signs of genetic manipulation or social experimentation.  Discover the fate of the colonists before the colony changes you.
  • Salvage Worth Risking: You’ve just been awoken from a dreamless hypersleep by MU/TH/UR, who has picked up something interesting on your sensors.  It might be worth a detour to scout it out, but the rest of the crew still slumbers...
  • A Ship You Know: The decrepit hulk adrift out here is a ship you recognize.  Board the vessel and determine its fate.
  • Something Stranger: This is an alien craft of unknowable make, impossible to separate from the yawning void around it.  It could have been drifting out here for centuries.  Whatever waits within could be worth a fortune...

Colonial Marine Missions

  • Escort Duty: Whatever is in the cargo hold must be worth something for the company to spring for a marine escort, even if its just one of you...
  • Beast On The Loose: The cargo contains an alien lifeform held in stasis.  But when the coolant system fails, it bursts from its prison and disappears into a maintenance hatch.
  • Alien Outbreak: It’s an alien pathogen sealed away in the hold, and upon its release, shit hits the fan.  Those who survive infection find themselves ...  changed.  Contain the outbreak, or escape before it claims you too.
  • Out Of The Frying Pan: You’ve left the fire, smoke, and blistering pulse rifle rounds behind for some much-needed R&R.  You catch a flight toward your destination, and settle in for an (ideally) uneventful trip back to civilization...
  • Pirate Attack: Opportunistic raiders seize a chance to loot the vessel, unaware of the presence of a Colonial Marine.  You alone now stand in their way – but you’re outnumbered and outgunned.
  • Engine Trouble: A ship-wide malfunction leaves you and the crew adrift in deep space.  Identify the problem and restore power to the ship.

Frontier Colonist Missions

  • Stowaway: There aren’t many chances for folk like you to get off-world and seek greener pastures – but you’ve seized an opportunity, stowing away aboard a departing vessel.  You emerge from your hiding place and find yourself alone...
  • Massacred Crew: You emerge to find a bloody scene.  The crew of the ship is dead, leaving you as the only apparent survivor.  Determine who or what killed the crew and avoid becoming the next casualty.
  • On The Hunt: You are not the only stowaway aboard this ship, and you soon become aware of something prowling the vents and tunnels, hunting the crew – and you.  Discover what it is and live to tell the tale.
  • Falling Star: A meteorite makes landfall near your home.  Recovering the meteorite, you and your fellow colonists find more than you bargained for...
  • Alien Object: The object defies logic, yet there it rests at the bottom of the crater.  Inscribed with indecipherable images and humming with innate power, the object is sure to change the course of your colony – for good or ill.
  • Lurking Presence: Something slumbers within the meteorite, an ancient malevolence that has known only the cold dark of space for untold eons.  Now it yearns for release.  What lies within, and can you survive its ire?

Company Rep Missions

  • Frontier Uprising: Discontented laborers have seized control of a Company station in orbit over a mining planet.  You are dispatched to help negotiate a settlement or otherwise quell the uprising.
  • Insurgent Infighting: The once-united rebels have fragmented over differing ideals and fight for control of the station.  Outlast the rebels or broker peace amid the chaos.
  • Falling Station: The rebels have cut critical systems in their bid for control, dropping the station into a dangerously low orbit.  Time is running out to retrieve valuable company assets.
  • Lost Company Property: An item invaluable to the Company has surfaced.  It is critical that you retrieve the item before other interested parties...
  • Flight Recorder: You arrive at a station to negotiate the return of a long-lost flight recorder, only to discover that the station’s leadership wants much more than expected in exchange...
  • Compromised Android: A Company facility lies in ruin, with multiple casualties and incalculable asset losses.  The only record of what transpired rests in the memory banks of an android, who has fled deep into the ruins to avoid retrieval.  Track the android and recover it – and its memories.

As an alternative to the sample missions listed above, you can use the Mother Analysis and Answer Matrices (see below) to quickly generate a spark of inspiration.  Rolling on the Complex Response Matrix will yield a simple story seed, such as “aid settlement” or “discover wreckage.”

DANGER LEVEL

THE LONGER YOU SURVIVE, the greater the dread and danger.  To help manage the pace of your mission, use the danger level.  It starts at zero, and maxes out at 10.  It determines the current danger phase:

DANGER LEVEL   PHASE   SITUATION
0-3   1   Low danger
4-7   2   Medium danger
8-10   3   High danger

The danger phase affects the result when you roll for a danger event (below), when setting the starting proximity on a danger timer (DANGER TIMERS ), and when adding potential complications on an objective check (Achieving An Objective ).  The danger level is increased as follows:

  • Encountering a danger event prompts you to increase the danger level by +1 or +2.
  • Triggering a danger timer (DANGER TIMERS ) increases the danger level by +1.  &

MOTHER ­ANALYSIS & ANSWER ­MATRICES

“I’ve got access to Mother now, and I’ll get my own answers, thank you.”
Lt.  Ellen Ripley  

When playing Last Survivor, you do so without a Game Mother.  In their place, you can use the Mother Analysis and Answer Matrices (MAAM) to help guide the way through your mission.

You needn’t use these tools each time you have a question in solo play.  Often, the answer will be obvious based on the situation.  When in doubt, err in favor of a dramatic, dangerous story.

2D6   RESULT
2   Roll for two danger events and danger level +2
3-4   Roll for one danger event and danger level +1
5-10   No event
11-12   Opportunity event (Opportunity Events )

Event Check

Through the course of your character’s mission, you’ll make event checks to add new and unexpected complications, troubling twists, or – more rarely – lucky breaks.  Make an event check when:

  • You roll on the Binary Response Matrix or Complex Response Matrix to ask a question or gain a detail.  If an event is triggered, resolve the answer to your question and the details of the event in whatever order you like.
  • You transition to a new scene with a time jump, move to a new location, or tie up a major element of your mission.  Whenever you are uncertain if the situation remains as-is or if there’s a wrench thrown in the works, make an event check.

To make an event check, roll 2D6 on the table above.  

Danger Events

Rolling a danger event on the event check table introduces a new or evolving complication in your mission.  Consider an event that fits the current situation or use the Danger Event Matrix below for inspirational prompts.  In addition, you must add +1 to your danger level when triggering a danger event.

You can also use the Danger Event Matrix whenever it feels like your session needs a jolt.  If you are ever unsure what happens next, increase the danger level by +1 and roll for a danger event to make something happen.

  • To determine your danger event, first roll D66 for the event focus and then 2D6 + current danger level for the event detail.

Opportunity Events

An opportunity event adds a positive twist or helpful asset to your mission.  Depending on the nature of your mission, this might serve as a milestone that triggers an objective check (Achieving An Objective).  An opportunity event is prompted by the event check table (Event Check).  In addition, you can introduce an opportunity event when a MAAM response indicates a positive twist is at-hand.  Such rewards should be rare.

Binary Responses

Use this tool when posing a question with a simple “yes” or “no” response, such as:

  • “Are there weapons stored in the cargo hold?”
  • “Does this dead guard carry a security keycard?”
  • “Is the artificial gravity functioning?”
If either answer is about equally likely, roll a D6.  If a “yes” response has a high probability, roll two D6s and take the highest result.  If a “no” has a high probability, roll two D6s and take the lowest.  If your PC has a stake in the situation, phrase your question so that a “yes” response is the most positive.  Check the adjacent Binary Response Matrix for your answer.

Rolling a “strong no” or “strong yes” response usually denotes additional details or unusual circumstances.  The answer to your question is unequivocal, and you discover or realize something more.

  • Your character explores a derelict settlement.  As your PC breaks into a locked storeroom, you ask the Binary Response Matrix if the compartment holds anything useful.  A “strong yes” might mean they have stumbled into a well-stocked armory, while a “strong no” could mean that the place has already been ransacked and cleared out.
  • Your character flees through the bowels of a ship.  As your PC rounds a corner, you ask the Binary Response Matrix if there are any good hiding spots in view.  A “strong yes” might reveal a hatch that can be sealed shut behind them, while a “strong no” could mean that your PC stares down a dead-end corridor.

1   Strong no
2-3   No
4-5   Yes
6   Strong yes

You can roll on a single column (Directive or Subject) for an answer, or roll on both columns to build a phrase.  You can take the result literally and apply it to your situation, interpret it to fit the context, or roll again for a more applicable answer.  >

Location Details

While playing as the Last Survivor, you spend much of your time envisioning the world around your PC, imagining the strobe-lit corridors of starships, the claustrophobic confines or orbital stations and planetary colonies, and the enigmatic environments of alien ruins or derelicts.

MULTIPLE    

WHEN ROLLING MULTIPLE    in a skill roll in solo play, either interpret the results and apply an appropriate narrative benefit, or choose a result from the adjacent table.  Choose and apply only one benefit per roll, even if you roll more than one additional    .

RESULT   EFFECT
Confident   Reduce stress level by –1.
Fast   Perform the action faster than expected.  If making a danger timer check (DANGER TIMERS ), roll –1 stress die.
Impressive   Impress others.  Gain +1 base die within this scene when using Empathy-based skills.
Intimidating   Cause enemies to falter or hesitate.  –1 base die for any skill rolls or attacks made against you.
Observant   Notice an important detail or clue.  Gain +1 base die on next skill roll that relates to acting on this information.
Skillful   Gain +1 base die on next skill roll.
Unnoticed   Perform the action with subtlety or stealth.  If making an encounter check or facing an OBSERVATION check by an NPC, –1 base die.

STRESS & PANIC

Stress Response

When playing Last Survivor, use the normal table for stress responses.  It’s repeated to the right for reference.

Panic Rolls

Use the below modified panic roll triggers for a solo PC.  More broadly, make a panic roll when you face a horrifying event, such as the death of an important character, a terrible discovery, or a dreadful complication that makes it seem as if all hope is lost.

  • You see a Xenomorph for the first time.
  • A Xenomorph comes within Adjacent range (even if you have seen it before).
  • Any other truly horrifying event occurs.

Solo Panic Response

When playing Last Survivor, use the alternative table on the for panic responses.

Stopping Panic

As in the standard rules, panic stops after you are broken or when a stretch passes.  In addition, since you don’t have fellow PCs to talk you down, you can use the presence and support of fellow NPC survivors to help stop panic.  To do so, make an Empathy roll.  If you are using a survivor timer (SURVIVOR TIMER) in your mission, you can add two base dice and one stress die to reflect their aid (see below).

RESULT   RESPONSE
≤0   Keeping Cool.  No effect.
1   Jumpy. When you push a skill roll, you gain +2 stress level instead of +1.
2   Tunnel Vision. All skill rolls based on Wits get –2 dice.
3   Aggravated. All skill rolls based on Empathy get –2 dice.
4   Shakes. All skill rolls based on Agility get –2 dice.
5   Frantic. All skill rolls based on Strength get –2 dice.
6   Deflated. You cannot push any skill rolls.  If you are Jumpy (#1 above), remove that response, and ignore any further Jumpy results while Deflated.  7+ Mess Up.  Your action fails regardless of rolled and you gain +1 stress level.
RESULT   RESPONSE
≤0   Keeping Cool.  No effect.
1   Spooked. Stress level +1.
2   Noisy. If you are hiding or attempting to sneak past an enemy, an NPC in the same zone will immediately detect you.  Encounter checks are made with +1 die.
3   Twitchy. Make an immediate supply roll for the gear that is most relevant to the current situation (air, ammo, or power).
4   Lose Item. You lose a weapon or other important item.  The GM decides which one.  In combat, you can pick up the item with a quick action.  Out of combat, you need an OBSERVATION roll and a stretch of time to find the item.
5   Indecisive. Make a check on any active danger timers.  If no timers are active, decide how your delay complicates the current situation.
6   Hesitant. You automatically get the #10 initiative card in combat until your panic stops.  If several PCs are Hesitant, draw the highest value cards randomly.
7   Freeze. You’re frozen by fear, losing your next turn and unable to perform any interrupt actions before then.
8   Seek Cover. You immediately seek (full) cover in the zone, if it is cluttered.  This is an interrupt action breaking the turn order.  Once in cover, your stress level is reduced 1 step, but you lose your next turn and are unable to perform any interrupt actions before then.  If you are in an open zone, you Scream instead (below).
9   Scream. You scream your lungs out, losing your next turn and unable to perform any interrupt actions before then.  Your stress level is reduced 1 step.
10   Flee. You immediately move away from the source of panic, into any adjacent zone, if such a move is possible.  This is an interrupt action breaking the turn order.  After the move, your stress level is reduced 1 step, but all friendly PCs in the starting zone get stress level +1.  
On your next turn and subsequent turns, you must spend all your actions to continue to move away, until you find a (reasonably) safe place, where you must remain until your panic stops.  You cannot perform interrupt actions before then.
If you cannot move out of your zone, you become Catatonic (result #12) instead.
11   Frenzy. You immediately attack the nearest person or creature, friendly or not.  Every friendly PC in the zone must make an immediate panic roll.  You won’t stop until you or the target is broken, or until your panic stops.  You cannot perform interrupt actions before then.
12+   Catatonic. You’re doomed! You collapse to the floor and can’t move, rambling or staring blankly into oblivion, until your panic stops.

DANGER TIMERS

“T-minus-45 minutes to impact event.”
MU/TH/UR 9000, Renaissance Station  

IN SOLO PLAY, danger timers tick away in the background for minutes or hours, counting down to new complications, frightening twists, and disastrous events.  Danger timers motivate a balance of speed and caution.  To keep the pressure on, always keep at least one timer running – especially when navigating or exploring a dangerous location.

Starting A Timer

To start a danger timer, first decide what event the timer will trigger when it counts down.  You may have a specific outcome in mind which fits the context of the mission thus far.  Otherwise, just flag a timer as “bad thing happens” and start the clock.  In that case, your PC has only a foreboding sense of impending doom, but lacks specifics.  You’ll find out together.

You can also look to a MAAM tool for inspiration.  Roll on the @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.tGNoaixXP7pVLIPq]{EV - 51.  LS - COMPLEX RESPONSE MATRIX}

and interpret the answer.  Or use the @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.TzDsXA9B8rSG6lyF]{EV - 48.  LS - DANGER EVENT MATRIX}

, choosing a result in the rightmost column as the event.

Next, give the event a proximity using the adjacent table.  If unsure, roll 2d6 to pick a proximity based on the current danger phase.

Checking Timers

Unlike the countdown timers described under Measuring Time, you needn’t make a check in each combat round for a danger timer.  Instead, check your active timers as time passes between scenes, when you encounter delays, when you move from one zone to another in stealth mode (STEALTH MODE ), or if you linger in an area or perform a complex task.

To check a danger timer, roll a number of stress dice according to the event proximity, as shown in the danger timer table.  For each    rolled, shift the event proximity closer by one step.  For example, from distant to approaching.  Repeat this check for each active timer.  As an event nears, you roll fewer dice when making a check – time seems to slow down, and every moment counts.  

If you are engaged in a lengthy scene or action, or if you take longer performing a task than expected, roll +1 stress die on each active timer to increase the chance of a timer advancing.  Similarly, if you manage to perform a task in less time than normal, roll –1 die (minimum one die).  Creeping or rushing in stealth mode (Choosing Your Approach ) also modifies the dice rolled by +1 and −1, respectively.

Triggering A Timer

When a danger timer drops to now, you have run out of time.  If you survive, do what you must to deal with the consequences.  If the timer was a placeholder for an unknown event, decide what happens (with the help of a MAAM tool if needed).  In addition, triggering a timer increases the danger level by one.

Stopping A Timer

Depending on the circumstances, you might have a chance to stop a timer.  For example, if you can reach the computer core before the ship self-destructs, you might convince Mother to stop the countdown.  Racing against time to avert a catastrophe is the perfect foundation for a solo scenario.

Once a timer is triggered or stopped – assuming your character survives and their mission continues – it’s time to add another.  Don’t let up.
