  • Creeping in stealth mode +1 die
  • Speedy actions −1 die (minimum 1)
  • Rushing in stealth mode −1 die (minimum 1)

Other Timers

Last Survivor uses three additional variations of timers: the survivor timer (detailed in the next section), an objective timer (OBJECTIVE TIMER ), and the encounter timer (Setting The Encounter Timer ).  These can function independently of – and alongside – one or more danger timers.  &

SURVIVOR TIMER

“We have twenty-five prisoners in this facility.”
Harry Andrews  

YOUR CHARACTER IS THE FOCUS of Last Survivor, but other characters might have a role in aiding your mission, or as the unfortunate victims of xenomorphs and other threats.  Rather than tracking Health and stress for friendly and neutral NPCs, you can use the survivor timer to gauge the group’s overall health, morale, and capabilities.

Setting The Survivor Timer

At the start of a mission that involves friendly or neutral NPCs, or when a group of NPCs is introduced, set the starting status on the survivor timer.

  • For a group of NPCs who are going about their duties unaware of the dangers to come, set the timer to unified.
  • If the NPCs are in the midst of a stressful situation, set the timer to strained.
  • If they have already faced casualties, set the timer to diminished.
STATUS STRESS DICE
Unified 6
Strained 5
Diminished 4
Overwhelmed 3
Desperate 2
Last Stand 1
You are the Last Survivor –
  • Expertise bonus: +2 base dice when survivors take actions suited to their role or capability.  If the situation favors them to a great degree, roll +3 base dice.

Survivor Check

Whenever survivors face a threat or attempt a dangerous action, make a survivor check by rolling the number of stress dice corresponding to their current status.  If they are performing an action suited to their particular role or capabilities, also roll +2 base dice as an expertise bonus.  If the situation favors them to a great degree, roll +3 base dice.  Then, interpret the result as follows.

  • If you roll one or more    , the survivors gain some measure of success – at least temporarily.  The more    rolled, the greater the success or impact on the scene.  When the survivors take action in a fight, convert each    to 2 points of damage and apply that damage to NPC enemies as appropriate.
  • If you roll one or more    , the survivors suffer setbacks.  For each    rolled, the status is shifted down by one step.  For example, from overwhelmed to desperate.  Depending on the situation, casualties can be interpreted as deaths, injuries, infighting, or panic – or some combination of those.  If unsure, ask the Binary Response Matrix.
  • A combination of    and    means the survivors achieved some success – but at a cost.

Aid From Survivors

When a group of survivors directly aids one of your skill tests in a dangerous situation, add two base dice and one stress die to your roll.  The extra dice represent the help provided by other survivors and the risk they are taking.

  •     are added to your roll as normal.
  • You can apply the impact of any    to the survivor timer instead of triggering a stress response for yourself.

Multiple Survivor Timers

If your mission involves multiple groups of friendly or neutral NPCs, you can use a separate survivor timer to track the status of each.

Off-Screen Survivors

When the action is entirely focused on your PC, it can be helpful to make occasional checks on the survivor timer to see how others are faring.  Make this check at least once per game session or per shift of in-game time.

  • If survivors are undertaking an extended, risky project, make the check using bonus base dice for expertise as normal.  This will determine both their success on the project and whether they suffer any casualties.
  • If the survivors are not taking on a risky project or directly engaging a threat, make the check using only stress dice.  Their expertise is not a factor.
  • If these checks indicate that the survivor timer shifts down, consider how these casualties manifest.

OBJECTIVE TIMER

“We have twenty-five prisoners in this facility.”
Harry Andrews  

Objective Timer

While danger timers and survivor timers represent an inevitable countdown to doom, objective timers help gauge the pursuit of your character’s mission-based goals.

You can also use the objective timer as a measure of your exploration or progress through a location when not using a map as a visual aid.  For each zone you traverse (using the guidelines under Using An Objective Timer ), make a check on the objective timer.

  • In your mission to retrieve the data from a lost flight recorder, you set an objective of “Find the flight recorder.” After you complete that objective and reclaim the recorder, you set a new objective of “Extract encoded data from flight recorder.”
  • As you wind your way through the bowels of a spaceship on the verge of critical failure, you set an objective of “Find an escape pod.” When the power fails and the pod won’t launch, you are sidetracked by a new objective: “Restore the ship’s power.”

Setting The Objective Timer

To start an objective timer, give it a name and a starting status: out of reach, far off, manageable, or near.  Your progress toward more distant objectives is slower, but they offer a higher experience reward once complete.

Progression

Whenever you make progress on an objective, make an objective check.  Roll a number of base dice corresponding to the objective’s current status.  For each    rolled, advance the timer one step.  For example, from near to within reach.  

If you fail to roll any    , consider how the objective remains unreachable, why this milestone fails to contribute meaningfully toward your goal, or what new minor complication crops up.

OBJECTIVE STATUS BASE DICE XP
Out Of Reach 1 6
Far Off 2 4
Manageable 3 2
Near 4 1
Within Reach 5 –
Achievable 6 –
Objective Reached – –
  • Medium Danger Swap in 1 stress die
  • High Danger Swap in 2 stress dice

Achieving An Objective

Once the objective timer drops to objective reached, your objective is at hand.  No other checks on the timer are necessary, although you might face skill rolls or encounters related to the nature of the objective.  For example, you reach the shuttle on the landing pad of the crumbling facility, but must still launch the vessel and escape.

When an objective is completed, you earn XP based on the starting status of the objective, as shown on the objective timer table.

Complications

When the danger level (DANGER LEVEL ) is medium, replace one of the base dice with a stress die as you make an objective check.  When it is high, swap in two stress dice.

  results cancel out    , one-for-one.  If you roll more    than    , you must also shift the objective one step higher.  For example, from manageable to far off.  Consider the nature of the complication, using the @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.tGNoaixXP7pVLIPq]{EV - 51.  LS - COMPLEX RESPONSE MATRIX}

for inspiration.  Overcoming this new complication can act as a milestone for your next objective check.

Failing An Objective

If an objective falls out of reach due to circumstances in your mission or choices made by your character, discard the timer.

SOLO STEALTH & ENCOUNTERS

“...  stay calm and stay quiet.”
Andy  

IN LAST SURVIVOR, an alternate stealth mode provides tools to navigate environments and trigger enemy encounters without a GM.  The solo stealth and encounter rules are used in tense exploration, stealth, or escape scenes where a hostile encounter might break out.  Movement from place to place without the chance of encountering an enemy should not be tracked and resolved at this level of detail.

Locations And Zones

A location represents a dangerous or unknown site, such as an alien derelict, abandoned station, or xenomorph-infested ship.  As with standard movement, a location is divided into zones (Zones ).

If you are using official maps for a location, use a token or miniature to track the location of your PC as you move from zone to zone.  You can also use the map to mark the location of suspected enemies or important objectives.

If you are playing without a map, zones act as an abstract measure of your movement from one area to another.  It may also help to sketch out a rough diagram as you proceed through a location, treating it like a flowchart of connecting zones.

Setting The Encounter Timer

When exploring an unknown location, or while attempting to search for, evade, or escape an enemy presence, use an encounter timer (below) to track the proximity of a potential encounter.

ENEMY PRESENCE STRESS DICE
All Clear 1
Uncertain 2
Suspected 3
Confirmed 4
Closing 5
Near 6
Encountered –
  • Making noise +1 die
  • Rushing +1 die
  • Creeping −1 die (minimum 1)

An encounter timer functions similarly to a danger timer (DANGER TIMERS ), but in reverse.  The number of dice you roll to check for an encounter increases as you explore a location.  Rolling on this timer is called an encounter check and is done when you move from zone to zone or linger in a zone.  The starting enemy presence should be set as best fits the circumstances.

  • If you are navigating an unknown location without any forewarning or suspicion of enemies, set it to all clear.
  • If there are known enemies, set it to confirmed to start.
  • If enemies are already converging on you, set it to closing or near.

Using An Objective Timer

Optionally, you can use an objective timer (OBJECTIVE TIMER ) to track your progress through a location, especially when playing without a map.  The timer will help set the pace of your exploration and mark the moment when you reach your objective.

Choosing Your Approach

Each time you move from one zone to another, decide your approach.

  • Stealthy: You are moving cautiously from zone to zone, keeping a low profile and remaining wary of dangers.  This is the default mode and has no effect on your die rolls.
  • Creeping: You are moving with abundant caution.  When you make an encounter check (Making Encounter Checks ), roll –1 stress die (to a minimum of 1).  When you roll OBSERVATION for your PC, gain +1 die, and any NPC using OBSERVATION to spot you loses –1 die.  However, your wariness comes at the cost of speed – you must make danger timer checks with +1 stress die.
  • Rushing: You attempt to outrun a deadline or flee from an enemy.  When you make an encounter check, add +1 stress die, and any OBSERVATION rolls made against you gain +1 die.  Your own OBSERVATION rolls are made with –1 die.  The good news? Your speed gives you an advantage against any danger timer checks, which are made with –1 stress die.

Making Encounter Checks

Make an encounter check as you move from one zone to another.  You should also make an encounter check if you linger in a zone for a stretch or longer to search or perform some other activity.

To make the check, roll a number of stress dice equal to the current enemy presence.  For each    rolled, shift the enemy presence one step closer.  For example, from confirmed to closing.  

If you are exploring a location without a known enemy, the progression of the encounter timer – at least until the later phases – represents subtle signs that someone or something else is in this place.  As the timer ticks down, the signs are more overt.

MODE ENCOUNTER CHECKS OBSERVATION ROLLS
BY YOU		 OBSERVATION ROLLS
AGAINST YOU		 DANGER TIMER CHECKS
Stealthy (default) – – – –
Creeping –1 die (min 1) +1 die –1 die +1 die
Rushing +1 die –1 die +1 die –1 die (min 1)

Sighting Enemies

You can use the number of    rolled on the encounter check as a gauge for the certainty that an enemy is near.  A single    is a subtle indication that others are in this location.  Two    is clear evidence that an enemy is drawing closer.  Three or more    is an unmistakable sign that you are in danger.

  ROLLED   EVIDENCE OF AN ENEMY PRESENCE
1   Imprecise pings on a motion tracker, vague sounds of movement, trails or tracks, evidence that someone has passed this way
2   Clear pings on a motion tracker, ­sightings of enemies on remote cameras, sounds coming nearer
3+   Urgent pings on motion tracker, ­shadows in your peripheral, nearby sounds, movement in the area

Triggering An Encounter

When you make an encounter check and shift the enemy presence to encountered, you must face a potential enemy.  If the nature of an encounter is obvious, make it happen.  Decide the specifics of the enemy you face and draw initiative.  If you’re not sure, use the encounter check to reveal additional details, as described below.

Revealing Encounter Details

The encounter check is multi-faceted.  After you’ve rolled the check, keep the dice and use the same roll to reveal additional details about the behavior of your enemy.

  • Using the highest die rolled, check the table for enemy behavior above.  This indicates who has the advantage at the start of the encounter.
  • Using the number of    rolled, consult the table for enemy threat below to gauge the severity of the threat.
HIGHEST DIE BEHAVIOR EFFECT
Stalking, hidden, or lying in wait NPCs automatically spot the PC.  PC rolls OBSERVATION to spot the NPCs.
5 Searching or hunting PC automatically spots the NPCs.  NPCs roll OBSERVATION to spot the PC.
4 Passive PC automatically spots the NPCs.  NPCs are unaware.
2–3 False alarm Non-hostile NPCs or unfounded fear.
Ambushing Draw initiative.  
PC is surprised.

Enemy Behavior

The above table helps determine the behavior of an enemy at the start of the encounter.  Check the highest stress die on your encounter check against the table below.

When playing Last Survivor, you can simply assume that zones are cluttered.  However, a map or the nature of an environment can lead to a different situation from one zone to the next.  If unsure if a zone is cluttered, ask the @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.6HcfWwkEJ1Y0KzMy]{EV - 50.  LS - BINARY RESPONSE MATRIX}, giving “yes” a high probability.

If the zone is open, the PC and the NPCs automatically spot each other at the start of the encounter.  You can ignore the listed effect and draw initiative. If the zone is cluttered, the effect result may force an OBSERVATION check for either the PC or NPCs.

As with the standard stealth gameplay (NPC Movement ), If one side remains unspotted, they may:

  • Reveal their presence.
  • Back out the way they came.
  • Ambush their foes.
  • Hide in the zone.

NPCs with the advantage should take the most sensible action at the start of an encounter.

Enemy Threat

When an encounter is triggered, consider what you know of the location, your mission, and potential enemies.  In most cases, the nature of the enemy will be obvious.

If you’re not sure, you can use the Binary Response Matrix, asking a question such as “Do I encounter a Xenomorph Drone?” or “Have the soldiers arrived?” Or use the adjacent table for enemy threats to gauge the strength or danger of the enemy, referencing the number of rolled on the encounter check.  Ask clarifying questions from there.

 ROLLED   THREAT   EXAMPLES
1   Lesser foe   Lone soldier or security guard, cultist, Xenomorph Facehugger
2   Greater enemy or group   Squad of marines, android, Xenomorph Drones
3+   Overwhelming enemy   Large force of soldiers, corporate assassin, ­Xeno­morph Queen

Avoiding An Encounter

If you remain unspotted once an encounter has occurred, you can attempt to avoid the enemy by hiding, backing out of the zone, or sneaking past them.

  • Hide: If you hide, decide whether the enemy makes an active search for you.  If unsure, ask the Binary Response Matrix.  If the enemies do search, make an OBSERVATION roll for them.  If they don’t search or fail to spot you, the enemies move out of the zone within a stretch of time.
  • Back Out: If you back out of the zone, you can do so without risk.  However, you should consider how this impacts the way forward within the location.  Retreating may not be an option.
  • Sneak Past: If you sneak past the enemies, make an OBSERVATION roll for them.  If their roll fails, you remain undetected and proceed to the next zone.

Once you’ve avoided an enemy, reset the encounter timer as described under Resetting The Encounter Timer.

Escaping An Encounter

When all else fails, and if you aren’t surprised by an encounter, you can attempt to flee before you are forced to draw initiative.  Escaping uses a MOBILITY roll.  Before rolling, consider any relevant factors that modify the number of base dice rolled as shown in the adjacent table.

  • If you succeed, you escape the encounter.  If using a map, place your character up to two zones away from your starting position.  Reset the encounter timer as described under Resetting The Encounter Timer.
  • On a failure, you are caught up in the encounter.  Draw initiative.  If using a map, place yourself and the enemies in the same zone or an adjacent zone.
FACTOR MODIFIER
You are outnumbered. –1
Fast movement is hampered by environmental conditions such as flooding or debris. –1
You are attempting to escape a speedy enemy, such as a Xenomorph. –2
Zero-G environment –2

Advancing Time

Check any active danger timers (DANGER TIMERS) after moving from zone to zone or lingering in a zone.  If your movement mode is creeping, roll +1 die.  If it is rushing, roll –1 die.  If you were caught up in an encounter, conducted a careful search, or suffered some other delay, also modify the timer check by rolling +1 die.  These modifiers stack.

Making Noise

If you cause excessive noise, you are more likely to alert enemies to your presence.  This can also happen by triggering the Noisy result on the panic response table (@TEXTDRAW[RollTable.fnb3mBmtREM3ccwW]{EV - 58.  LS - SOLO PANIC RESPONSE TABLE}).  When making noise, add +1 die to encounter checks until you stop and move at least two zones away.  If you are rushing, this die stacks – giving you +2 dice on your encounter checks.

Using A Motion Tracker

As enemies move within range, a functioning motion tracker gives you a better chance of outmaneuvering and spotting those enemies.  If you roll at least one    and no more than one    on an encounter check without triggering an encounter, you may choose one of these two options instead of rolling for the next encounter check.

  1. Outmaneuver: If the enemy presence is confirmed or greater (or closing or greater for a limited-range motion tracker such as the M314), shift the current enemy presence one rank farther as you move to an adjacent zone.  For example, from near to closing.  You are using the signal to put distance between you and the enemy.
  2. Prepare: If the enemy presence is closing or near, you may immediately shift the enemy presence to encountered and ignore the spotting effects of the table for enemy behavior.  You automatically spot the NPCs, and they must make an OBSERVATION roll to spot you.

Resetting The Encounter Timer

When an encounter is avoided, escaped, or resolved, reset the encounter timer as best fits the situation.

  • If you faced and defeated a singular enemy or have no reason to believe other enemies are in this location, set the timer to all clear.
  • If you presume that enemies remain in this location, but aren’t sure, set the timer to suspected.
  • > If you are certain that enemies are still somewhere in the location, set the timer to confirmed.  If you believe they are in the vicinity, make it closing.

You should also reset the encounter timer anytime the situation changes dramatically or if you gain a notable advantage that puts distance between you and potential enemies.

Revealing Details

As you move from zone to zone, take a moment to consider your surroundings.  What is the function of this area? What dangers or opportunities does it introduce? If you are using a map, check the visual for insight.  Otherwise, use MAAM tools such as the location detail matrices (Location Details ) to fill in the blanks.

Searching And Scavenging

Make an OBSERVATION check when searching an area.  If you are looking for something specific, the check will reveal if it is found.  If you are generally searching for useful items or hidden details, use the Salvage Matrix (Under Location Details ) to reveal what you uncover as follows.

 ROLLED   SALVAGE
0   Nothing useful found and time wasted.
1   Roll for a common item on the Salvage Matrix.
2   Choose a common item on the Salvage Matrix or roll for a rare item.
3+   Choose a common or rare item on the Salvage Matrix.

Alternatively, with one or more successes, you can roll on the Complex Response Matrix (Under Location Details ) and interpret the answer.

Searching takes time, a stretch or more, and should trigger danger timer checks or additional dice on those checks as appropriate.  If you spend your successes to perform a search faster instead of giving you more options, you can make the danger timer check with –1 stress die.  &

SOLO COMBAT

Combat for a Last Survivor is managed as in standard play, although you’ll need to take on the duties of a GM in determining NPC actions and making rolls for NPCs.  Here are a few guidelines:

  • Draw initiative as normal for your PC and any NPCs.  Draw a single initiative card for groups of NPCs.
  • When an NPC acts against or aids your character, roll for their action as a GM would.  As with standard play, NPCs never push rolls and do not have a stress level.
  • When deciding actions for an NPC in a fight, choose whatever is most sensible and expected in the current circumstances.  If unsure, ask the Binary Response Matrix.  For example, “Does the soldier use a quick action to defend?”
  • When an NPC performs an action that doesn’t directly affect your PC, you can simply decide if they are successful.  If it’s dramatic and dangerous, make it happen.  If unsure, ask the Binary Response Matrix.
  • Human NPCs are typically concerned with self-preservation.  If things go against them, they act defensively or flee.  Use the Binary Response Matrix to check their willingness to fight, giving sensible responses a high probability as appropriate.
  • Xenomorphs close to Adjacent range and use their signature attacks.  They never dodge or defend in close combat.  When they are reduced to zero health, roll on the broken Xenomorph table (THE XENOMORPHS ) to see what happens.

SOLO SPACE COMBAT

If you find yourself caught up in a space battle, you can instead use the simplified system detailed below.

Objectives

First, set an objective timer (OBJECTIVE TIMER ) for your ship and crew.  Decide your goal for the battle and make the status manageable for an evenly matched fight, near if you have a clear advantage, or far off if you are outmatched.  Then, decide what the enemy seeks to accomplish in the battle – such as boarding, disabling, or destroying your ship – and set a danger timer (DANGER TIMERS ) to track their progress.  Roll for a proximity using the current danger phase.

If unsure of an enemy objective, consider the most likely and interesting goal.

Phases

Once those pieces are in place, the battle proceeds in stretches – divided into four phases.

  1. Action Phase: Make a skill roll for your character that reflects your focus or the station you are manning.  For example, PILOTING if at the controls, COMTECH if using the sensors to lock or spoof an enemy ship, or COMMAND if leading others.  See the list of crew positions on for a summary of roles and skills.
  2. Ship Phase: Make an objective check to represent the actions of the crew and the capabilities of your ship.  Add one additional base die for each    gained on your roll in the previous step.  For each    , advance the objective timer one step.  If you reach your objective, the battle is won, and your goal is achieved.
  3. Enemy Phase: Roll on the danger timer for the enemy.  For each   rolled, advance the timer one step.  If the timer reaches now, the enemy wins the battle.  As appropriate to their goal, your ship might be destroyed, disabled, boarded, or left in their wake.
  4. Damage Phase: Optionally, if the enemy is armed, you can use the component damage tables (Ship Damage ) to help detail the hits taken by your ship.  Whenever the danger timer advances by a step, roll two stress dice and consult the following table.
 ROLLED   DAMAGE
0   Damage to armor and hull.
1   Minor component damage.
2   Major component damage.  A lucky hard hit can lead to catastrophic damage before the timer runs out.

If the objective timer and danger timer are both still active, the battle continues.  Repeat the phases above.  Along the way, consider the details of the battle as revealed by the dice results.  Your character may need to change stations or deal with new compications as the battle progresses.

UPGRADES

THIS EVOLVED EDITION of the ALIEN RPG core rulebook can be used with game material for the first edition of the game, such as cinematic adventures and campaign books, with just a few tweaks.  This appendix gives you the tools you need to upgrade the material to the Evolved Edition.

Talents

A small number of talents have been replaced in the Evolved Edition.  If an NPC or pre-generated PC has a talent not present in this book, simply replace it with another talent of your choice.

Weapons

Some modules for the first edition, especially the campaign books, include several new weapons.  If the same weapon appears in this book as well, use the stats in this book.  If not, you can use the stats as they stand, but you will need to add an ammo capacity for each weapon, as that stat did not exist in the first edition.  See the table below for guidance.

CORE RULES - HOW TO USE THIS MODULE.name: CORE RULES - HOW TO USE THIS MODULE
CORE RULES - HOW TO USE THIS MODULE
CORE RULES - HOW TO USE THIS MODULE.text:
Welcome to the Alien Evolved
Core Rules Module.

If you are new to the Alien RPG system make sure you check out the @UUID[JournalEntry.SkwfSOD5gNvLhaLv]{MU/TH/ER Instructions.} Journal which can be found in Compendiums>Mother Instructions. This contains a quick guide to using the Alien RPG system.


Alien Evolved Core Rules

All you need to run a game is imported and organised into folders for each of the asset types.

You can rerun the import script at any time by going to Configure Settings> Module Settings and hitting the import button. Any existing assets will not be overwritten so it's useful if you accidentally delete something.


Scenes

Organised into Two folders:

  • Alien RPG Mother Aids: contains general background images to share with players.
    The "ToM - Meeting Room" scene is designed as a "Theatre of the Mind" map to use as a staging area for the players while dealing with the narrative aspects of the scenario. There is an invisible wall across the lower part of the map.
    The PCs are placed here which allows them to access their character sheets, make rolls etc.
    The upper portion is for the GM to put NPCs giving the same control.

  • Alien RPG Novgorod Station 3 scenes for Novgorod Station.
    Each scene has light blocking walls and doors and FoW enabled to provide a more immersive experience when the players are moving around the map.
    There is no lighting on these maps so you may wish to add this.


Actors

In order to maintain compatibility with the Classic edition all new Evolved assets are in the "Alien Evolved" folder.
Creatures has folders for Creatures, Territories and Vehicles which contain all the assets from the Core Rules.

NPCs:
Folder containing the NPC templates
For the Skill-Stunts rolldown (clicking on the spanners next to the skill) will show all the skill stunt options as per the rules.
Similarly clicking on the Talent name will show the details for that talent.


Where NPCs have Items these are set to "Inactive" so will need to be activated (left mouse click on the item image) by the player/GM to be used.


Items

In order to maintain compatibility with the Classic edition all new Evolved assets are in the "Alien Evolved" folder.
Under the "Alien Evolved" folder:

  • Armor: all the armor in the Core Rules.
  • Weapons: all the weapons in the Core Rules.
  • Equipment: all the equipment in the Core Rules.
  • Talents(Career): all the Career Talents in the Core Rules.
  • Talents(General): the General Talents in the Core Rules.
  • Vehicle Weapons: all the Vehicle Weapons in the Core Rules.

Other folders

  • Alien RPG Systems: all the Star Systems in the Core Rules.
  • Alien RPG Spaceship Modules: spaceship modules and accessories.
  • Alien RPG Spaceship Weapons: spaceship weapons and accessories.

As with the core system just drag and drop the items on to the character sheets as required


Journals

Under the "Alien Evolved" folder:
Alien Evolved Player Guide the player rules section journals This can be shared with players.

Alien Evolved GM Guide the GM rules section journals This should not be shared with players.

Alien RPG Systems Journals Journal entries for each of the systems that can be dragged onto the "Stars of the Middle Heavens" scene. There is also a template that can be copied and editied to create your own systems.

The Art of Alien: Contains journal entries of images from the rule book you can display to your players at any point during your games. The Alien Rules has some fantastic artwork so I could not leave it out!!


Tables

The Core Rules builds on the table structure set up by the core system and adds many new roll tables from the book to the structure.

In order to preserve compatibility with older modules the Evolved all tables begin with "EV - "

All Creature macros are available in the drop down menu when you create a new Creature.

You can access these directly but using the macros supplied with the system makes the game flow faster.

Remember when the results are displayed in the chat window and there is a "roll for attack" shown you can click on the dice image to display the number of successes.    

Macros

The Alien system comes with 4 macros that will help you run the game smoothly.

  1. Alien - GM Dice Roller: Allows you to perform ad-hoc dice rolls. Uncheck the GM Only box to make the rolls public.
  2. Alien - Player Ad-hoc YZE Dice Roller: Make this available to your players. They need to have a token selected before running the macro.
  3. Alien - Roll on selected Mother table v10: provides a drop down listing all the Mother Tables available. Allows multiple rolls against the table and modifiers (+/- x to roll not additional dice).
  4. Alien - Roll on selected Creature table v10: same as above for Creature tables but no modifiers and all rolls are private to the GM.

Life Paths.name: Life Paths
Life Paths.text:
THIS LIFE PATH GENERATOR randomly determines most aspects of your PC’s early life, with a few choices for you to make along the way. The circumstances and events revealed by the dice form the framework of your PC’s backstory, leaving you to interpret those events and fill in the gaps in any way you want.

The life path system produces a wide variety of character outcomes and histories and can result in unbalanced PCs. However, there is huge enjoyment in playing a PC whose backstory has dealt them a challenging hand, especially when your PC overcomes their disadvantages to prove the doubters wrong.

The life path does not use the concept of a key attribute, but your choice of career still defines the skills and talents available to you.

Life Path Generation - Follow these steps to determine the life path of your character:

  1. Determine if you are human or an android. Roll 2D6. On a result of 11 or 12, you are an android. If you are an android, decide with your GM if you are a secret android.

  2. Roll for your origin and gain 3 points in random general skills.

  3. Determine your early life, gaining 2 attribute points and 2 skill points.

  4. Experience a life event – roll to see what befalls you and gain 2 more attribute points and 2 points in random general skills.

  5. Gain 2 points in attributes of your choice and then apply for your first career.
    If successful, you gain 2 points in random career skills, a roll for gear, and a roll for your first paycheck.

  6. Serve your first term – roll to see where you were posted and how well you performed. You gain 1 more point in a random career skill, a random talent, another roll for gear, and another paycheck roll.

  7. Did you want to serve a second and third term? Follow the same process for your first term, but for each extra term you must reduce an attribute of your choice by 1 point.

  8. Get your psych evaluation.

  9. The final touches – your PC’s name, appearance, age, personal agenda, signature item, buddy and rival.

Base Attribute Scores

Humans start with a base score of 2 in each attribute. Androids may add +3 to two attributes of their choice before starting their life path. Don’t worry about the low scores – you gain more attribute points as you progress through life.

Maximum And Minimum Scores

By the end of the life path, a human PC must have a score of at least 2 in every attribute and cannot have any score greater than 5.Android PCs can finish their life paths with attribute scores up to 8.Skill levels can never exceed 5 for any PC. If the random life path roll results in an attribute score or skill level outside of the allowed range, re-roll or choose another result.

1. Human or Android?

Determine if you are human or an android. Roll 2D6. On a result of 11 or 12, you are an android. If you are an android, decide with your GM if you are a secret android.

2. Origin

Which super-nation were you born into or which one made you? What is your corporate or government sub-affiliation? Where do you call home? Roll 2D6 on the table below to find out, then D6 twice for your sub-affiliation and home. Finally, gain 3 points in random general skills.

@TEXTDRAW[RollTable.ckBj1KxpjnoXK0aR]{EV - 31. LIFE PATH - ORIGIN}

@TEXTDRAW[RollTable.8OOJbb2EmTuLZcxC]{EV - 34. LIFE PATH - RANDOM GENERAL SKILLS}

3. Early Life

What was your early life like, who did you share it with, and what experiences did you have?
Roll D66 three times on the table below, once for each column, and add the specified attribute and skill points (2 of each) to your scores. Decide the precise details of your early life experience, depending on whether you are human or an android. You may also gain modifiers to your psych evaluation roll – note these as you go.

@TEXTDRAW[RollTable.SCl1BZa4oHjMeZ4Q]{EV - 32. LIFE PATH - EARLY LIFE}

4. Life Event

Your life event can take place at any point in the lifepath of your choosing, but is decided now by a D66 roll on the table below. These events offer story hooks and may leave a lasting impact on your PC – the impact should be roleplayed. Agree to the specific details of any event with your GM. Your life event gives you 2 specified attribute points and 2 points in random general skills.

@TEXTDRAW[RollTable.RCUQjuMAO69J32Ad]{EV - 33. LIFE PATH - LIFE EVENT}

@TEXTDRAW[RollTable.8OOJbb2EmTuLZcxC]{EV - 34. LIFE PATH - RANDOM GENERAL SKILLS}

5. Career

Next, gain 2 points in attributes of your choice and then apply for your first career. The table below lists the minimum attribute scores for each career. To apply, make a skill roll against one of the skills listed for the career. The roll cannot be pushed.

  • If unsuccessful, you are rejected and must apply to a different career (however, you may pull a fast one).

  • If you roll one you join as a standard recruit.

  • If you roll two or more someone has noted your potential, and you gain a favor – make a roll on the table later in this chapter.

  • Pull a Fast One
    If you fail an application, you can pull a fast one. Your PC does something underhanded or illegal to get around the system, or begs a favor from someone in the hierarchy – settle the details with the GM. Your previously unsuccessful roll now counts as one success, and you’re in! But a dangerous secret now hangs over you, or you owe someone a big favor.

  • Playing a Kid
    The Kid is not a career, it’s a lifestyle. You don’t need to apply to play a Kid, you may just choose this career. However, Kids are limited to only one term for their career, while the other careers can be extended up to three terms

You’re Hired!

Once recruited, you go into basic training, get geared up, and get your first paycheck.

  • Roll D3 twice on the table below for career skills, gaining 1 skill level for each roll.

  • Roll once on the gear table for your career (see chapter 2). Re-roll if you roll an item you already have.

  • Roll for your first paycheck.

    6-7. Career Terms

You must serve at least one term in your career but may choose to serve up to three (with the exception of the Kid career, which can only serve one).

Follow these steps for each term:

  1. Posting: What did you do during this term?
    Roll D6 on the relevant table for your career to find out. This can give you a bonus gear roll, and you also gain 1 point in a random career skill.
    @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.4hQBGuyR69LJwMl0]{EV - 40. LIFE PATH - POSTINGS KID}
    @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.gJd4w751LTItNJpp]{EV - 41. LIFE PATH - POSTINGS MEDIC}
    @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.eWlxxVQ5SNpL9BaY]{EV - 42. LIFE PATH - POSTINGS OFFICER}

    @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.WgV5SdFyKdjKPLks]{EV - 45. LIFE PATH - POSTINGS SCIENTIST}

  2. Performance: How well did you do your job?
    Make a skill test against a career skill of your choice (you cannot push):

  • If you fail, you suffer a disaster (roll on the table below) and get –1 on your psych evaluation roll.

  • If you roll one your performance has been satisfactory.

  • If you roll two or more you have performed well and gain a favor (roll on the table below) and get +1 on your psych evaluation roll. Re-reroll any favors you already have.

  1. Skillpoint: Gain 1 more skill point in a random career skill. *NB seems to be omitted from the rule book, although it is stated in the lifepath overview*

  2. Talent: Gain one random career talent.
    For your second and third term, you may replace this with a general talent of your choice.

  3. Gear & Paycheck: Make one roll for career gear. Re-roll any items you already have and make a paycheck roll.

7. Another Term?

Should you choose to serve another term, follow the process for the first term again (6). However, subtract 1 point from an attribute of your choice for each extra term you serve – getting older and weather-beaten does that to you.

8. Psych Evaluation

Each character ends their life path with their psych evaluation, so the company can see what they’ve got on their hands. Androids undergo a “product cognitive stability test,” and also roll on the table. Players should roleplay the results. Roll 2D6 on the table below and apply any modifiers you gained during your life path.

@TEXTDRAW[RollTable.eJgLp3u3A5HAAHuY]{EV - 46. LIFE PATH - PSYCH EVALUATION}

9. Final Touches

Decide your character’s name, appearance, age, personal agenda, signature item, and buddies & rivals. To complete this, keep in mind that your PC’s formative and life events may drive their personal agenda. Good luck out there – you’re gonna need it.

Last Survivor Crib Sheet.name: Last Survivor Crib Sheet
Last Survivor Crib Sheet.text:
This journal is intended to provide quick access to the key tables for Last Survivor.

Clicking on the links to the tables will do a normal roll.

Pressing [shift] + [left mouse] will pop-up a modifier box allowing you to apply modifiers to the roll the roll (Danger Level, etc.).

Refer to Last Survivor chapter for the full procedure.

Event Check

Through the course of your character’s mission, you’ll make event checks to add new and unexpected complications, troubling twists, or – more rarely – lucky breaks.  Make an event check when:

  • You roll on the Binary Response Matrix or Complex Response Matrix to ask a question or gain a detail.  If an event is triggered, resolve the answer to your question and the details of the event in whatever order you like.
  • You transition to a new scene with a time jump, move to a new location, or tie up a major element of your mission.  Whenever you are uncertain if the situation remains as-is or if there’s a wrench thrown in the works, make an event check.

To make an event check, roll @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.y5qBxs7g2yOxQBFk]{EV - 47. LS - EVENT CHECK}.  

Danger Events

Rolling a danger event on the event check table introduces a new or evolving complication in your mission.  Consider an event that fits the current situation or use the Danger Event Matrix below for inspirational prompts.  In addition, you must add +1 to your danger level when triggering a danger event.

You can also use the Danger Event Matrix whenever it feels like your session needs a jolt.  If you are ever unsure what happens next, increase the danger level by +1 and roll for a danger event to make something happen.

  • To determine your danger event, first roll on @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.TzDsXA9B8rSG6lyF]{EV - 48. LS - DANGER EVENT MATRIX} for the event focus. Then click on "Roll on Danger Event Detail Table" and in the pop-up enter the current Danger Level.

If the event doesn’t fit your mission or situation, check adjacent rows for inspiration.  Or just choose a focus and roll for the event details.

Opportunity Events

An opportunity event adds a positive twist or helpful asset to your mission.  Depending on the nature of your mission, this might serve as a milestone that triggers an objective check (Achieving An Objective).  An opportunity event is prompted by the event check table (Event Check).  In addition, you can introduce an opportunity event when a MAAM response indicates a positive twist is at-hand.  Such rewards should be rare.

@TEXTDRAW[RollTable.4noZ8O5EW3a7N5H3]{EV - 49. LS - OPPORTUNITY EVENT MATRIX}

Binary Responses

Use this tool(@TEXTDRAW[RollTable.6HcfWwkEJ1Y0KzMy]{EV - 50. LS - BINARY RESPONSE MATRIX}) when posing a question with a simple “yes” or “no” response, such as:

  • “Are there weapons stored in the cargo hold?”
  • “Does this dead guard carry a security keycard?”
  • “Is the artificial gravity functioning?”

If either answer is about equally likely, roll a D6.  If a “yes” response has a high probability, roll two D6s and take the highest result.  If a “no” has a high probability, roll two D6s and take the lowest.  If your PC has a stake in the situation, phrase your question so that a “yes” response is the most positive.  Check the adjacent Binary Response Matrix for your answer.

Rolling a “strong no” or “strong yes” response usually denotes additional details or unusual circumstances.  The answer to your question is unequivocal, and you discover or realize something more.

  • Your character explores a derelict settlement.  As your PC breaks into a locked storeroom, you ask the Binary Response Matrix if the compartment holds anything useful.  A “strong yes” might mean they have stumbled into a well-stocked armory, while a “strong no” could mean that the place has already been ransacked and cleared out.
  • Your character flees through the bowels of a ship.  As your PC rounds a corner, you ask the Binary Response Matrix if there are any good hiding spots in view.  A “strong yes” might reveal a hatch that can be sealed shut behind them, while a “strong no” could mean that your PC stares down a dead-end corridor.

Complex Responses

Throughout your sessions of Last Survivor, you may find yourself asking nuanced, open-ended questions that necessitate more than a simple “yes” or “no” answer.  In these cases, the @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.tGNoaixXP7pVLIPq]{EV - 51. LS - COMPLEX RESPONSE MATRIX} provides more descriptive, thematic answers that you can apply based on the current situation, mission, and environment.

You can roll on a single column (Directive or Subject) for an answer, or roll on both columns to build a phrase.  You can take the result literally and apply it to your situation, interpret it to fit the context, or roll again for a more applicable answer.  >

Location Details

While playing as the Last Survivor, you spend much of your time envisioning the world around your PC, imagining the strobe-lit corridors of starships, the claustrophobic confines or orbital stations and planetary colonies, and the enigmatic environments of alien ruins or derelicts.

When you need inspiration, use the following tables.  They offer aspects and discoveries for some commonly explored locations.  They include:

  • Use the @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.dnm74JBwOH9AMQ6v]{EV - 52. LS - SECTION MATRIX}: table when you are exploring a human starship, orbital station, or colony to help reveal the purpose of an area.  The answer should offer clues for what you would typically see or find there.
  • Use the @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.YnhWA69wqLLp2jsB]{EV - 53. LS - ACCESS MATRIX}: table to reveal the connection between sections of a human starship, orbital station, or colony.  This can help if mapping out a location or imagining the potential obstacles when traversing from one section to the next.
  • Use the @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.mTOYRNuf40Sq8r6J]{EV - 54. LS - ENVIRONMENT MATRIX}: table for a descriptive prompt for an area within a human starship, orbital station, or colony.  The answer may reveal mundane details or unexpected mysteries or obstacles.
  • Use the @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.37Ev57rL1z1MvKaL]{EV - 55. LS - SALVAGE}Matrix: table when searching or scrounging within a human starship, orbital station, or colony.
  • Use the @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.6xrRGeiWodnTPYOV]{EV - 56. LP - ANOMALOUS ENVIRONMENT MATRIX}: for details observed when exploring an alien derelict or ruin, or while navigating a ship or facility transformed by Xeno­morphs or biological corruption.

STRESS & PANIC

Stress Response

When playing Last Survivor, use the normal table for @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.djNUi4dXjUY8dGrV]{EV - 57. LS - SOLO STRESS RESPONSE TABLE}.

Panic Rolls

Use the below modified panic roll triggers for a solo PC.  More broadly, make a panic roll when you face a horrifying event, such as the death of an important character, a terrible discovery, or a dreadful complication that makes it seem as if all hope is lost.

  • You see a Xenomorph for the first time.
  • A Xenomorph comes within Adjacent range (even if you have seen it before).
  • Any other truly horrifying event occurs.

Solo Panic Response

When playing Last Survivor, use the alternative @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.fnb3mBmtREM3ccwW]{EV - 58. LS - SOLO PANIC RESPONSE TABLE}.

Stopping Panic

As in the standard rules, panic stops after you are broken or when a stretch passes.  In addition, since you don’t have fellow PCs to talk you down, you can use the presence and support of fellow NPC survivors to help stop panic.  To do so, make an Empathy roll.  If you are using a survivor timer (SURVIVOR TIMER) in your mission, you can add two base dice and one stress die to reflect their aid (see below).

DANGER TIMERS

“T-minus-45 minutes to impact event.”

MU/TH/UR 9000, Renaissance Station  

IN SOLO PLAY, danger timers tick away in the background for minutes or hours, counting down to new complications, frightening twists, and disastrous events.  Danger timers motivate a balance of speed and caution.  To keep the pressure on, always keep at least one timer running – especially when navigating or exploring a dangerous location.

Starting A Timer

To start a danger timer, first decide what event the timer will trigger when it counts down.  You may have a specific outcome in mind which fits the context of the mission thus far.  Otherwise, just flag a timer as “bad thing happens” and start the clock.  In that case, your PC has only a foreboding sense of impending doom, but lacks specifics.  You’ll find out together.

You can also look to a MAAM tool for inspiration.  Roll on the @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.tGNoaixXP7pVLIPq]{EV - 51.  LS - COMPLEX RESPONSE MATRIX} and interpret the answer.  Or use the @TEXTDRAW[RollTable.TzDsXA9B8rSG6lyF]{EV - 48.  LS - DANGER EVENT MATRIX}, choosing a result in the rightmost column as the event.

Next, give the event a proximity using the adjacent table.  If unsure, roll 2d6 to pick a proximity based on the current danger phase.

Checking Timers

Unlike the countdown timers described under Measuring Time, you needn’t make a check in each combat round for a danger timer.  Instead, check your active timers as time passes between scenes, when you encounter delays, when you move from one zone to another in stealth mode (STEALTH MODE), or if you linger in an area or perform a complex task.

To check a danger timer, roll a number of stress dice according to the event proximity, as shown in the danger timer table.  For each    rolled, shift the event proximity closer by one step.  For example, from distant to approaching.  Repeat this check for each active timer.  As an event nears, you roll fewer dice when making a check – time seems to slow down, and every moment counts.  

If you are engaged in a lengthy scene or action, or if you take longer performing a task than expected, roll +1 stress die on each active timer to increase the chance of a timer advancing.  Similarly, if you manage to perform a task in less time than normal, roll –1 die (minimum one die).  Creeping or rushing in stealth mode (Choosing Your Approach) also modifies the dice rolled by +1 and −1, respectively.

Triggering A Timer

When a danger timer drops to now, you have run out of time.  If you survive, do what you must to deal with the consequences.  If the timer was a placeholder for an unknown event, decide what happens (with the help of a MAAM tool if needed).  In addition, triggering a timer increases the danger level by one.

Stopping A Timer

Depending on the circumstances, you might have a chance to stop a timer.  For example, if you can reach the computer core before the ship self-destructs, you might convince Mother to stop the countdown.  Racing against time to avert a catastrophe is the perfect foundation for a solo scenario.

Once a timer is triggered or stopped – assuming your character survives and their mission continues – it’s time to add another.  Don’t let up.

1-1.description: Driver Hit: The driver is hit and suffers damage equal to the damage inflicted on the vehicle

2-2.description: Passenger Hit: A random passenger is hit and suffers damage equal to the damage inflicted on the vehicle. Re-roll if no passengers are present.

3-3.description: Severe Spin: The attack rocks the vehicle. The driver must make an immediate Piloting roll (not an action)-failure means that the vehicle is Wrecked.

4-4.description: Weapon Disabled: A random weapon mounted on the vehicle is disabled. Re-roll if no weapons are present.

5-5.description: Engine Disabled: The engine is disabled, and the vehicle can't continue. An aerial vehicle can make a controlled landing, losing one zone of altitude per Round.

6-6.description: Fuel Explosion: The vehicle explodes in a ball of flame. All people inside it are immediately exposed to intensity 9 fire, and the vehicle is destroyed beyond repair.

1-1.name: Spooked.
1-1.description: Stress level +1 for you.

2-2.name: Noisy.
2-2.description: Any enemies nearby (GM’s discretion) are automatically alerted to your presence.

3-3.name: Twitchy.
3-3.description: Make an immediate supply roll for air, ammo, or power (GM’s discretion).

4-4.name: Lose Item.
4-4.description:
You lose a weapon or other important item. The GM decides which one. In combat, you can pick up the item with a quick action.

Out of combat, you need an OBSERVATION roll and a stretch of time to find the item.

5-5.name: Paranoid.
5-5.description: You cannot give or receive help on skill rolls until panic ends.

6-6.name: Hesitant.
6-6.description: You automatically get the #10 initiative card in combat until your panic stops. If several PCs are Hesitant, draw the highest value cards randomly.

7-7.name: Freeze.
7-7.description: You’re frozen by fear, losing your next turn and unable to perform any interrupt actions before then.

8-8.name: Seek Cover.
8-8.description:
You immediately seek (full) cover in the zone, if it is cluttered. This is an interrupt action breaking the turn order.

Once in cover, your stress level is reduced 1 step, but you lose your next turn and are unable to perform any interrupt actions before then.

If you are in an open zone, you Scream instead.

9-9.name: Scream.
9-9.description:
You scream your lungs out, losing your next turn and unable to perform any interrupt actions before then.

Your stress level is reduced 1 step, but every friendly PC in the zone must make an immediate panic roll.

10-10.name: Flee.
10-10.description:
You immediately move away from the source of panic, into any adjacent zone, if such a move is possible.

This is an interrupt action breaking the turn order.

After the move, your stress level is reduced 1 step, but all friendly PCs in the starting zone get stress level +1.

On your next turn and subsequent turns, you must spend all your actions to continue to move away, until you find a (reasonably) safe place, where you must remain until your panic stops. You cannot perform interrupt actions before then.

If you cannot move out of your zone, you become Catatonic (result #12) instead.

11-11.name: Frenzy.
11-11.description:
You immediately attack the nearest person or creature, friendly or not. Every friendly PC in the zone must make an immediate panic roll.

You won’t stop until you or the target is broken, or until your panic stops. You cannot perform interrupt actions before then.

12-20.name: Catatonic.
12-20.description: You’re doomed! You collapse to the floor and can’t move, rambling or staring blankly into oblivion, until your panic stops.

1-1.name: Jumpy.
1-1.description: When you push a skill roll, you gain +2 stress level instead of +1.

2-2.name: Tunnel Vision.
2-2.description: All skill rolls based on Wits get –2 dice.

3-3.name: Aggravated.
3-3.description: All skill rolls based on Empathy get –2 dice.

4-4.name: Shakes.
4-4.description: All skill rolls based on Agility get –2 dice.

5-5.name: Frantic.
5-5.description: All skill rolls based on Strength get –2 dice.

6-6.name: Deflated.
6-6.description: You cannot push any skill rolls. If you are Jumpy (#1 above), remove that response, and ignore any further Jumpy results while Deflated.

7-10.name: Mess Up.
7-10.description: Your action fails regardless of rolled and you gain +1 stress level.

1-3.description: Escape: With a snarl the Chestburster flees, moving two zones away in one action, into the nearest vent, sewer or duct if possible. As soon as the PC's lose line of sight the Chestburster has escaped. Stealth mode ensues as the Chestburster tries to hide and grow.

4-4.description: Terrorizing Hiss: The Chestburster jumps towards a target, flashing its razor-sharp teeth and hissing malevolently. The target must make an immediate panic roll. The Imp will instead mimic the actions of the target in an unsettling manner, with the same effect.

5-5.description:
Leg Slash: With a snarl the Chestburster slashes its target's leg, metallic teeth flashing in the light.

Roll for the attack using [[6db]] Base Dice, Damage 2.

If the attack causes damage, it automatically inflicts critical injury #53 (even if the victim is not Broken), triggering an immediate Panic Roll.

6-6.description: Throat Bite: The Chestburster squeals a high-pitched shriek and goes for the throat. Roll for the attack with eight base dice, base damage 1, armor piercing. If the attack causes damage, it triggers an immediate panic roll.

1-2.name: Skittering Menace:
1-2.description: Skittering Menace: The Facehugger has chosen its host! It skitters forward, single- minded and horrifyingly spider-like. The victim gains stress level +1 and must make an immediate panic roll. The next attack from the Facehugger will be against the same target with +1 to the[[1db]] roll.

3-4.description: Tail Grapple: The Facehugger leaps and catches its victim, its tail whipping violently.
3-4.name: EV - Sub Table Facehugger Attacks

5-5.description:
Face Grapple: The Facehugger leaps at its victim’s face with horrifying speed. Roll for an attack with six base dice. It’s possible to defend against the attack.

If the attack hits, the target must make an immediate panic roll, and the Facehugger will perform The Final Embrace (result #6) on the same target on its next turn.

6-6.description:
The Final Embrace: The Facehugger gets to its victim, its acid making short work of any helmet or respirator in the way (armor has no effect, except the APEsuit.

Roll for the attack with eight base dice [[8db]].

It’s possible to defend against the attack.

If the attack hits, the poor victim is facehugged and immediately broken. Their last sensations are horrible, yet strangely loving: a firm but gentle caress around their head, a smothering sensation followed by a warm burst of oxygen-rich air filling their lungs, a deep sensation of slow-motion falling, it’s okay to fall asleep…

1-1.description:
Sonar Sweep: The Harvester takes in its surroundings by singing out a quick sonar pulse.

Add +1 to the next roll on this table (for a maximum of 6).

All PCs within Long range get stress level +1.

2-2.description:
Sonar Pulse: The Harvester uses its sonar as a weapon.

Everyone within Short range gets blasted by the ultra-sonic burst and must make a STAMINA roll (no action) or be stunned and lose their next turn.

3-3.description:
Charge: The Harvester rushes the enemy it deems to be the biggest threat. It makes a manic charge against it and continues into the next zone.

Roll for the attack with six base dice [[6db]], base damage 3, armor piercing.

The attack can be dodged, but not defended against.

4-4.description:
Stampede: The Harvester goes berserk, like a bucking bronco, and flails around in a maddened frenzy.

All targets in the zone suffer a crushing attack of eight base dice [[8db]], base damage 2.

5-5.description:
Burrowing Claws: The beast’s claws are almost as bad as its maw, and it leaps on a poor victim.

It suffers an attack with ten base dice [[10db]], base damage 2, armor piercing.

6-6.description:
Pulverize: The victim is dragged into the beast’s dreadful meat-grinder of a mouth.

Roll for the attack with eight base dice [[8db]], base damage 2, armor piercing.

If damage is inflicted, the victim dies, its body mercilessly minced and its agonized screams ringing in the ears of their friends.

1-1.description:
Intimidating Display: The Lion Worm rears up, its golden cilia flowing in threatening patterns. But it’s a bluff.

The expert predator has seen a problem and is using an aggressive display to cover a tactical retreat.

All PCs within Short range must make a panic roll.

On its next turn, the Lion Worm attempts to leave combat and stealth mode resumes. When it makes its next attack, it gets a +1 to its roll on this table (to a maximum of 6).

2-2.description:
Playing With Its Prey: The Lion Worm attacks but for fun, rather than to kill.

Roll for the attack with eight base dice [[8db]].

If the attack hits, the target drops a weapon (or other item) of the GM*s choice, but is otherwise unharmed.

The Worm rears over them, wishing for its prey to run before it attacks again. The victim must make an immediate panic roll.

3-3.description: Acrid Pheromones: The Lion Worm releases a huge dump of pheromones into the air. They are so pungent that anyone near the creature starts to cough, and all PCs within Short range must make a STAMINA roll (no action) or lose their next turn.

4-4.description:
Feral Rage: The beast attacks, throwing everything at its victim, with ten base dice [[10db]], base damage 2.

If it causes any damage, its insatiable desire to kill allows it to immediately make a second attack, with the same effect.

5-5.description:
Crippling Attack: The Lion Worm attacks to incapacitate its target, either to eat later or get enough space to escape a bad situation.

It goes for a crippling blow, making an attack with eight base dice [[8db]], base damage 1, armor piercing.

If it does any damage, the victim is automatically broken.

6-6.description:
Death Roll: The Lion Worm goes full out for the kill, grasping its target and wrapping it in a vicious death roll.

Roll for the attack with ten base dice [[10db]], base damage 1, armor piercing.

If the attack hits, the victim is grappled (page 62) and must win an opposed roll for CLOSE COMBAT against the Lion Worm’s MOBILITY to break loose.

On its next turn, the Lion Worm squeezes the victim, attacking with ten Base Dice [[10db]], base damage 1 again.

This continues until the victim is killed or breaks free.

1-1.description:
Terrifying Hiss: The Neomorph leans in close to the victim (Adjacent range), showing its razor-sharp teeth and hissing.

The victim must make an immediate panic roll.

2-2.description:
Tail Slash: The Neomorph pivots, slashing its victim with its sharp tail.

The victim is attacked using ten base dice [[10db]], base damage 2.

3-3.description:
Deadly Grab: The Neomorph jumps at its victim, grabbing it and dragging it away.

Roll for the attack using eight base dice [[8db]], base damage 1.

If it hits, the Neomorph immediately drags the victim into an adjacent zone (free bonus move), dumping it on the floor.

The victim drops a weapon (or other item) and must make an immediate panic roll.

4-4.description:
Leaping Attack: The Neomorph jumps at the victim.

Roll for the attack using eight base dice [[8db]], base damage 1.

If the attack is successful, the victim is thrown to the ground and must make an immediate panic roll, and the Neomorph immediately performs a free extra attack with ten base dice [[10db]], base damage 2.

5-5.description:
Tail Spike: The Neomorph impales the victim with its razor-sharp tail.

Roll for the attack with ten base dice [[10db]], base damage 2, armor piercing.

6-6.description:
Throat Bite: The Neomorph bites the victim’s throat.

Roll for the attack using eight base dice [[8db]], base damage 1, armor piercing.

If the attack causes damage on a human, it kills the victim outright.

1-3.description:
Escape: With a snarl, the Bloodburster flees, moving two zones away in a single action, into the nearest air duct if possible. As soon as the PCs lose line of sight, combat ends and stealth mode ensues.

After [[1d6]] stretches, the Bloodburster grows into a Juvenile Neomorph and starts stalking the PCs.

4-4.description:
Terrifying Hiss: The Bloodburster jumps onto the victim, showing its razor-sharp teeth and hissing.

The victim must make an immediate panic roll.

5-5.description:
Leg Bite: With a snarl, the Bloodburster bites the victim’s leg.

Roll for the attack using six base dice [[6db]], base damage 2.

If the attack causes damage, the victim immedi- ately suffers an Impaled Thigh critical injury even if not broken.

6-6.description:
Throat Bit: The Bloodburster bites the victim’s throat.

Roll for the attack with eight base dice [[8db]], base damage 1, armor piercing.

If the attack causes damage on a human, it triggers an immediate panic roll.

EV - Praetorian, Charger and Queen Attac.name: EV - Praetorian, Charger and Queen Attacks

1-1.description: Call The Guard: The enormous Xenomorph lets out a shrill cry for help, calling [[3db]] Sentries (for the Queen) or Soldiers (for the Praetorian or Charger) to its defense. They arrive in the following round, then draw initiative and can act.

2-2.description:
Frenzy: The Xeno leaps at its enemies, sweeping its arms, legs and tail through their ranks.

All targets in the zone are knocked prone, take 1 point of damage, and must make immediate panic rolls.

The effect is automatic, but the attack can be dodged with a successful MOBILITY roll, avoiding all effects.

3-3.description:
Beastly Bite: The Xenomorph takes a huge bite from its victim.

The attack is rolled with ten Base Dice [[10db]], Damage 1, armor piercing.

If the attack causes any damage on a human, the victim is automatically broken.

4-4.description:
Charge: Charger/Queen only (re-roll for Praetorian).

Roll for the attack with eight base dice [[8db]], base damage 4 (2 for a Queen), armor piercing.

The attack can be dodged, but not defended against.

5-5.description:
Tail Spike: The Xenomorph impales the victim with its razor-sharp tail.

Roll for the attack with twelve base dice [[12db]], base damage 2, armor piercing.

6-6.description:
Headbite: The Xenomorph opens its outer jaws wide, and the deadly inner jaws lean out, gnashing in anticipation before snapping forwards.

The attack has a strength of eleven base dice [[11db]], base damage 2, armor piercing.

If it causes any damage on a human, it automatically kills the victim in one dreadful blow.

1-1.description:
Call For Reinforcements: The Xenomorph pauses, hissing quietly but all the more threatening for that.

It looks like it’s thinking, or maybe giving silent orders to unseen companions. Then, another Xenomorph appears in an adjacent zone, ready to act in the next round.

All PCs in sight of it get stress level +1.

2-2.description:
Frenzy: The Xeno leaps at its enemies, sweeping its arms, legs and tail through their ranks.

All targets in the zone are knocked prone, take 1 point of damage, and must make an immediate panic roll.

The effect is automatic but the attack can be dodged with a successful MOBILITY roll, avoiding all effects.

3-3.description:
Talon Attack: The Xenomorph launches into a wild attack with its large, clawed talons at its victim.

Roll for the attack with twelve base dice [[12db]], base damage 1, armor piercing.

4-4.description:
Capture For The Hive: The Xenomorph attacks with its venom-spiked tail, with twelve base dice [[12db]], base damage 1, armor piercing.

If the attack causes any damage, just 1 point of damage is inflicted, and the paralyzing venom takes effect. The victim must make a STAMINA roll – the number of successes rolled is the number of rounds it can stay up, then it falls unconscious for one shift.

The victim can be woken up with a MEDICAL AID roll (full action) by another character – otherwise the Xeno captures the victim for the hive, placing it by an Ovomorph to be facehugged at a dramatically appropriate time.

5-5.description:
Tail Spike: The Xenomorph impales the victim with its razor-sharp tail.

Roll for the attack with eleven base dice [[11db]], base damage 2, armor piercing.

6-6.description:
Headbite: The Xenomorph opens its outer jaws wide, and the deadly inner jaws lean out, gnashing in anticipation before snapping forwards.

The attack has a strength of ten base dice [[10db]], base damage 2, armor piercing.

If it causes any damage on a human, it automatically kills the victim in one dreadful blow.

EV - Stalker, Scout and Drone Attacks.name: EV - Stalker, Scout and Drone Attacks

1-1.description: Hypnotizing Gaze: The Xenomorph, eyeless as it may seem, stares deeply into the soul of its victim. The victim is mesmerized by the dread beauty of such a beast. They stand in awe of what nature, or god, or the devil has created, get +1 STRESS LEVEL and must make an immediate Panic Roll.

2-2.description: Playing With Its Prey: The Xeno attacks, but not to kill. The victim is knocked down and drops a weapon (or other item) of the GM’s choice, but otherwise takes no damage. The Xenomorph stands over its prey, taunting them to run so the game can go on. The victim must make an immediate panic roll.

3-3.description: Deadly Grab: The beast launches through the air, grabbing its victim with its talons. It attacks with eight base dice, base damage 1. If it hits, the Xeno immediately drags the victim into an adjacent zone (free bonus move), dumping it on the floor. The victim drops a weapon (or other item) of the GM’s choice and must make an immediate panic roll.

4-4.description: Ready to Kill: The Xenomorph grabs its victim with its talons, its inner jaws poised to strike. Roll for the attack with ten base dice. If it hits, the victim takes 1 point of damage and is grappled and must win an opposed roll for CLOSE COMBAT against the Xeno’s MOBILITY to break loose. All friendly characters in the same zone must make a panic roll. Unless the victim breaks free, the Xenomorph will use a Headbite attack (#6 below) on its next turn.

5-5.description:
Tail Spike: The Xenomorph impales the victim with its razor-sharp tail.

Roll for the attack with ten base dice [[10db]], base damage 2, armor piercing.

6-6.description:
Headbite. The Xenomorph opens its outer jaws wide, and the deadly inner jaws lean out, gnashing in anticipation before snapping forwards.

The attack has nine base dice [[9db]], base damage 2, armor piercing.

If it causes any damage on a human, it automatically kills the victim in one dreadful blow. However, should the GM wish it, the victim remains just alive enough for the Xenomorph to initiate the ovomorphing process.

EV - Sub Table Facehugger Attacks.name: EV - Sub Table Facehugger Attacks
EV - Sub Table Facehugger Attacks.description: Sub RollTable for "4 Tail Grapple" Facehugger Attacks

1-2.description: The victim’s legs are caught and it falls down, making an immediate panic roll and is unable to move until the Facehugger makes another action or is killed.

3-4.description: The victim’s arm gets hopelessly tangled in the beast’s tail. The victim drops one weapon (or other item) of the GM’s choice and must make an immediate panic roll.

5-6.description: The Facehugger wraps its tail around the victim’s neck, choking it – it must make an immediate panic roll and roll for STAMINA or suffer 1 point of damage (armor has no effect).

1-1.description:
Consume: The Swarm consumes everything in its path, and this place is rich in food.

The Swarm’s Health is restored by 2 points, making it harder to drive off.

2-2.description:
Pheromones: The Swarm is getting increasingly agitated and more and more pheromones are being released into the air.

The Swarm’s next roll on this table gets +1.

3-3.description:
Suffocating Swarm: The swarming creatures are everywhere. They are in the victims’ eyes, ears and mouths, and it is almost impossible to breathe.

Everyone inside the Swarm area must make a STAMINA roll.

Failure means the victim loses their next turn, and the Swarm will perform a Stripped To The Bone attack against one victim on its next turn.

4-4.description:
Desperate Hunger: The Swarm is so hungry it will eat anything, and right now the polymers and compounds in the players’ armor look good.

Everyone within the Swarm wearing armor suffers an attack rolled with eight base dice [[8db]], base damage 1.

Any damage is immediately subtracted from the armor level. Those not wearing armor find their clothes have been shredded, but the attack does not inflict any damage.

5-5.description:
Feeding Frenzy: The Swarm is hungry and tries to eat anything it can envelope.

All characters inside the Swarm suffer an attack rolled with six base dice [[6db]], base damage 1, armor piercing (as the creatures look for ways to slip past it).

6-6.description:
Stripped To The Bone: The Swarm focuses on one target, and that victim takes an attack rolled with twelve base dice [[12db]], base damage 1, armor piercing.

If the attack inflicts any damage, the Swarm will automatically attack the target again on its next turn.

This will continue until an attack fails to inflict damage, the victim is stripped to the bone, rescued, or the Swarm is driven off.

1-1.description:
Retreat: The Scorpionid isn’t stupid and won’t fight unless there’s a good reason to.

On this occasion it decides to flee the fight as quickly as possible.

2-2.description:
Pinned Down: The Scorpionid uses its powerful pincers to pin down its target.

Roll for the attack using ten base dice [[10db]], base damage 1.

If the attack hits, the target drops a weapon (or other item) and must make an immediate panic roll.

3-3.description:
Pincer Grab: The creature tries to seize its victim in its enormous claws, quivering with the anticipation of a quick strike with its huge tail.

Roll for the attack with eight base dice [[8db]], base damage 1.

If the attack hits, the victim is grappled and must win an opposed roll for CLOSE COMBAT against the Scorpionid’s MOBILITY to break loose.

If the Scorpionid retains its grasp, it will automatically make a Tail Strike attack against the victim on its next turn.

If this attack hits underwater, the Scorpionid will also drag the victim deeper and one zone away from the group, causing them to also suffer the effects of drowning.

4-4.description:
Flailing Strike: The Scorpionid’s pincer swipes at its target.

Roll for the attack with eight base dice [[8db]], base damage 1.

If the attack hits, the Scorpionid flings the victim into the next zone, causing another point of damage.

5-5.description:
Tail Strike: The Scorpionid swings its terrible tail forward with deadly purpose.

It attacks with ten base dice [[10db]], base damage 1, armor piercing.

If it inflicts any damage, it also poisons the victim with a deadly venom, counting as a disease with a virulence rating of –2.

6-6.description:
Immobilize: The Scorpionid wants to escape, but to do so it needs to take its attackers out of the fight.

It lunges for its victim’s legs with its huge claws, making an attack with eight base dice [[8db]], base damage 2.

If it does any damage, the victim immediately suffers an Impaled Thigh critical injury even if not broken.

11-15.description: Mayday Before (or after) the starship is in hyperspace, the crew receive a distress signal and are obliged by law to assist. Alternatively, the call may come whilst on-planet.

16-22.description: Bad Intel Key mission information will prove false or very misleading.

23-25.description: Sabotage A serious malfunction or crisis (fire, etc.) quickly turns out to be sabotage, but who is the saboteur?

26-35.description: Secret Plot NPCs or PCs in the game have another agenda that runs counter to that of the players and they are busy working on it.

36-43.description: Murder An NPC is suddenly murdered. Who did it? Why?

44-46.description: Flare Event A burst of stellar radiation reaches the PCs’ location from a red dwarf flare star, a distant neutron star or other phenomenon. This could cause power interruptions, or at the very least complete communications blackouts.

51-55.description: Malfunction A key component to the mission fails when needed – an airlock or drive, a demolitions charge or diamond cutting drill. What now?

56-64.description: Time Limit The mission has a deadline; lives (perhaps their own) are depending on it.

65-66.description: Xenomorph Outbreak. At the heart of this scenario is the presence of the Xenomorph XX121. It may be one egg or dozens, or the massacred remains of an unfortunate group of humans with a Xenomorph warrior still on the prowl. Good luck...

2-2.name: REACTION
2-2.description: UNUSUAL. May be on an unusual trajectory, have the registration of a missing ship or simply refuse to respond to the PCs’ signals.

3-4.name: REACTION
3-4.description: DISMISSIVE. If asked for information or assistance, the ship will decline.

5-8.name: REACTION
5-8.description: RADIO SILENCE. Ignores the PCs’ ship, but polite if contacted.

9-10.name: REACTION
9-10.description: FRIENDLY. May pass on information or advice, if relevant.

11-11.name: REACTION

12-12.name: REACTION
12-12.description: FAMILIAR VESSEL. The ship is known to you, you may even know the crew.
